title: Reliability
text:
R
You need to learn about the following R functions:



R
Description




alpha()
Cronbach’s alpha



The function alpha() is part of the psych package.
Examples:
Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for unstandardized items item1-item10:

psych::alpha(
  data |> select(item1:item10)
)

Standardized items, sign of each item as is:

psych::alpha(
  data |> select(item1:item10),
  check.keys = FALSE
)

Store a scale as a new variable:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    SR = rowMeans(
      select(., item1:item10),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

Display item statistics and alpha if item deleted:

psych::alpha(
  data |> select(item1:item10)
)

The output includes Cronbach’s alpha, item-total correlations, and the value of alpha if each item is deleted in turn.

title: Reliability
text:
Assignments

Use the dataset sbs399_sexroles. We assess the reliability for the sex role items in this dataset.


Check the descriptives of the sex role items sexrol1-sexrol5, including the number of missing values for each of the variables.
Do a reliability analysis of the standardized items, keeping the items directed as in the data. What is the value (estimate) of Cronbach’s alpha?
Check the alpha’s if each item is deleted from the scale in turn. The deletion of which item will increase the reliability? Why?

Hint: Verify that it is negatively correlated to the other items and should be recoded first.

Reverse item 5 and redo the analysis. What is the value of Cronbach’s alpha now?
Check the alpha’s if items are deleted. The deletion of which item will increase the reliability? Is this increase large? Discuss the advantage and drawback of deleting this item. For instance, one drawback of deleting an item is the decrease in the range of attitude measures.
What is the sample size in the data and what is the sample size in the analysis?
Replace the missing values for a variable with the mean of this variable. Do again a reliability analysis. Notice that the reliability goes down. Why will this be the case? What would be a better imputation for the missing values?


Use the dataset muslimrights. We now assess the reliability for scales in this dataset. Refer to your results in the section on factor analysis. We want to assess the reliability of the two factors of the two-dimensional solution and the reliability of the unidimensional solution.


Do again the factor analysis with an oblique rotation. Notice that two items are difficult to place: items 2 and 7.
Assess reliability separately for items 1 to 4 and for items 5 to 7. What happens to the reliability if you delete items 2 and 7?
Do a reliability analysis for items 1 to 7 together. What happens if you delete items 2 and 7?

title: Creating new variables
text: In this part you will learn about the following basic tasks:

title: Creating new variables
text:
R
To create or modify existing variables in a dataset, we will use the function mutate().
The table below shows useful functions for recoding variables. These functions are normally used within mutate().







Function
Description




if_else()
Create/modify based on simple logical condition


case_when()
Create/modify based on multiple logical conditions


recode_values()
Recode values (dplyr version >= 1.2)


replace_values()
Replace values (dplyr version >= 1.2)


across()
Applies function to multiple columns



Examples:
Create a variable as a mathematical expression of existing variables:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    hhinc = h_inc + w_inc,
    minc = (h_inc + w_inc) / 2,
    adiff = abs(age - page),
    inc2 = inc^2
  )
# sum, mean, absolute difference, and squared income (^ denotes "power")

Change negative values of an existing variable:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    inc = if_else(inc < 0, 0, inc)
  )
# replace negative of values of inc by 0

Create a binary (“dummy”) variable:

# Create binary variable male. 
# Suppose that sex is coded as female=1, male=2, and there are no missings

# The variable can be numerical (0/1)..
data |>
  mutate(
    male = if_else(sex == 2, 1, 0) # male = 1, female = 0. In thise case, we could also simply do `male = sex - 1`
  )

# or logical (TRUE/FALSE)...
data |>
  mutate(
    male = (sex == 2) # male = TRUE, female = FALSE
  )

For many uses in R, having a binary variable as numeric (1/0) or logical (TRUE/FALSE) makes little difference. For example, R will treat TRUE/FALSE as 1/0 if you compute the mean of a logical vector. Logical binary variables can make code a bit more succint when they are used in other operations: with logical vectors you can write e.g filter(male, employed) instead of filter(male == 1, employed == 1). But be aware that some mathematical and modelling functions expect only numerical variables.
In the code above, we presumed thhat there were no missing values. If there were missing values, they would be coded as 0, which is obviously wrong. To deal with with missing values:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    male = recode_values(sex,
                         1 ~ 0,
                         2 ~ 1) # Change 1 into 0, 2 into 1
  )
# By default, recode_values() assigns missing (NA) to any values we did not specify. So any NAs would stay as NAs, and any values otehr than 1 and 2 would become NA).

Recode a dummy variable:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    female = 1 - male
  )
# male = 1 becomes female = 0 and vice versa
# NA values remain NA

Recode values into categories:

# create region variable
# 71, 72, 79 = 1
# 73 to 78 = 2
# all other valide (non NA) codes = 3
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    region = recode_values(country,
                            c(71, 72, 79)  ~ 1,
                            73:78          ~ 2,
                            NA ~ NA,
                            default = 3 # this applies to all other values not speficied above. 
                                        # Attention: if we had nto specified NA ~ NA above, 
                                        # NA values would also have been recoded to 3
    )
  )

You can also recode using case_when(), specifying logical conditions instead of original values on the lef-hand side. case_when() is thus more flexible (e.g. it can handle conditions based on multiple original variables, see below) but tends to more verbose.

# Same task as above, using case_when().
# Note that we explicitly refer to the original variable in each condition
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    region = case_when(
      country %in% c(71, 72, 79) ~ 1,
      country %in% 73:78         ~ 2,
      !is.na(country)            ~ 3,
      is.na(country)             ~ NA
    )
  )


# Recoding based on multiple existing variables
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    group = case_when(
      (male==1 & age < 18)  ~ "male_minor",
      (male==1 & age >= 18) ~ "male_adult"
      (male==0 & age < 18)  ~ "female_minor",
      (male==0 & age >= 18) ~ "female_adult"
      .default              ~ NA  # Everything else as NA. Note the dot in .default.
    )
  )

Create a standardized variable (z-scores):

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    zedu = (edu - mean(edu, na.rm = TRUE)) /
      sd(edu, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# standardize edu

Create a rank variable:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    rinc = rank(inc)
  )
# rank order statistics of income

With across() you can repeat operations across several columns:

# Create a new variable counting the number of variables with value == 2:
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    ngood = rowSums(
      across(good01:good05, ~ .x == 2), # for each variable good1 to good5, check if the value is 2
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

# Change 9999 to NA in all variables whose names start with "income" 
data <- data |>
  mutate(
         across(starts_with("income"), ~if_else(.x == 9999, NA, .x))
         )

title: Creating new variables
text:
Assignments

1. Create dummy variables.
In the dataset sbs399 the variable class marks the respondent’s social class. How often is this variable non-missing?
We want to create a dummy variable for being of white collar. This variable, which we will call white, is 1 for subjects belonging to the white-collar class and 0 otherwise. We interpret missing values in class to denote “unknown”. Thus, the dummy white should also be missing if class is missing.

Create this dummy variable using if_else(). Call it white1.
Create the same dummy variable using recode_values(). Call it white2.
Produce a cross-tabulation of the two newly created variables and verify that they are identical.



2. Recoding a categorical variable.
In the dataset sbs399 the variable polit marks the political party the respondent intended to vote for in a national election.

Generate a new variable pol_pref in which political preference is expressed on a left-to-right scale:

1 = SP
2 = GroenLinks
3 = PvdA
4 = D66
5 = CDA
6 = VVD
7 = GPV
8 = RPF
9 = SGP
10 = Unie 55+
11 = AOV
12 = CD

Recode pol_pref into a new variable pol_pref3 in which political preference is expressed in three categories:

1 = Left (SP, GroenLinks, PvdA, D66)
2 = Center (CDA)
3 = Right (all remaining parties)


3. Recode a continuous variable into groups.
We consider the hourly wage variable hrinc.
Generate a new variable hrinc_quart for the four quartiles of hrinc:

hrinc_quart = 1 for the lowest 25%
hrinc_quart = 2 for the next 25%
hrinc_quart = 3 for the next 25%
hrinc_quart = 4 for the highest 25%

Verify that the groups contain approximately equal numbers of observations.


4. Centering and standardizing variables.
We focus on hrinc again.

Create a variable c_hrinc that contains the centered hourly wage rate by subtracting the sample mean of hrinc. Check that:


the mean of c_hrinc is approximately 0;
the standard deviations of c_hrinc and hrinc are the same.


Create a variable z_hrinc that contains the standardized hourly wage rate by subtracting the mean of hrinc and dividing by its standard deviation. Check that:


the mean of z_hrinc is approximately 0;
the standard deviation of z_hrinc is approximately 1.


Create a variable z2_hrinc that standardizes hourly income separately for men and women. Within each sex, the mean of z2_hrinc should be approximately 0 and standard deviation approximately 1. Ensure that:


you obtain one variable, not two;
the variable is not missing unless hrinc itself is missing.


Apply a unit-range transformation to hrinc:

\[U(x) = \frac{x - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)}\]

Verify that the transformed minimum equals 0 and the transformed maximum equals 1.

Which method do you prefer for income? And for number of hours worked per week?


5. Creating scales
We consider the five items sexrol1 to sexrol5 in the dataset sbs399. These items measure attitudes towards women’s emancipation by (5 point) Likert items. We want to average the 5 items and treat it as a measurement of attitude, with a larger value indicating a more traditional attitude.

Explain why it is not sensible to simply add the five items.
You likely want to reverse one of the items. Which one? Construct a new variable for this reversed item using:


a recoding approach with recode_values() (or case_when());
a mathematical expression. Verify that both constructed variables are identical.


Create the attitude measure from the five items. Hint: use rowMeans(). What is the mean of the measure? Can you interpret this mean substantively?
The data used so far are complete, meaning that respondents answered all items. In many surveys, however, respondents do not answer every question. This situation is illustrated by the dataset sbs399_sexroles. We will now discuss a simple ad hoc method to deal with this. This method is quick-and-dirty; it used to be widely used, but theoretical statistics has yielded better methods. We will discuss these more advanced methods later on.

For now we simply take the mean of all valid item responses for each respondent. Thus, if a respondent answered items 1, 2, and 3, but not items 4 and 5, we calculate the scale score as the mean of items 1, 2, and 3. If a respondent answered all items, we take the mean across all items. If a respondent did not answer any of the items, the scale score should be missing as well.
In R, this can be accomplished using the argument na.rm = TRUE in rowMeans() (or in mean() used together with rowwise()), which computes the mean using all available values while ignoring missing values.

title: Dealing with missing data
text: As one of the more serious of the ten plagues of the social sciences, we now turn to missing values. We will not discuss extensively how to deal with missing values in a statistically appropriate way. Suppose you want to fit a regression model of Y on X1 and X2. What should you do if Y, X1, or X2 are sometimes missing? Some possible approaches:

title: Dealing with missing data
text:
R
In this part you need to learn about the following R functions and packages:



Function
Description




na_if()
Recode values to missing


replace_na()
Recode missing to values


is.na()
Test whether values are missing


vis_miss()
Description and visualization of missing values



Examples:
Create a dummy variable for whether educ is missing:

data <- data |>
  mutate(educ_mv = is.na(educ))
# educ_mv is a logical dummy (TRUE/FALSE)

Create a dummy male, set to missing if sex is missing:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    male = if_else(sex == 1, 1, 0)
  )
# assumes sex == 1 is male
# if_else() propagates NA from its condition: when sex is NA, the condition
# sex == 1 is also NA, so male becomes NA automatically.

List edu for observations for which age and country are not missing:

data |>
  filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(country)) |>
  select(edu)

Recode the values 98 and 99 of edu into missing values:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    edu = na_if(edu, 98),
    edu = na_if(edu, 99)
  )

Recode missing values to 99:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    edu = replace_na(edu, 99)
  )

Count the number of missing values in a variable:

data$educ |>
  is.na() |>
  sum()

Count the number of missing values per variable in a series of variables:

data |>
  summarise(
    across(starts_with("good"), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))
  )

skimr::skim() gives the same information, together with other descriptive statistics, for any set of selected variables:

library(skimr)

data |>
  select(starts_with("good")) |>
  skim()
# the n_missing and complete_rate columns report missingness per variable

Display missing value patterns and their frequency in a series of variables:

library(visdat)

data |>
  select(good01:good05) |>
  vis_miss()

title: Dealing with missing data
text:
Assignments

Use the dataset hin95_educ.


How many missing values are there in the variable educ?
Create a dummy variable indicating whether educ is missing.
Create a copy of educ with missing values set to 99.
Create a new imputed variable, replacing the missing values by the unconditional mean of educ over the observed values.
Create another new imputed variable, replacing the missing values in educ by the gender-specific conditional means of educ over the observed values. Thus, for men we impute the mean of educ for men, and for women we impute the mean of educ for women.
Compare the means and standard deviations of the three versions of the original variable educ and the two imputed versions. Reflect on eventual differences.


(Advanced, assumes you already know regression analysis) You may also replace the missing values in a variable y by the predicted values of y on some appropriate explanatory variables. As an example, perform a regression of a respondent’s educ on the education of the respondent’s father, feduc, the education of the respondent’s mother, meduc, and gender, sex. Replace missing values in educ by the predicted values of this regression. Explain why educ still has missing values. Any suggestions how to proceed?
Consider the variables rs280 to rs286 in the dataset hin95.


Create a variable counting the number of non-missing values in this series of variables. How many observations have no missing values on any of these variables? How many observations have exactly one missing value? How many observations are always missing in this series?
Now select the observations without missing values. Generate a variable with the mean of these variables. What is the mean of this mean-variable?
In the original dataset, create a variable with the mean over the available values. Thus, if for an observation the variables v1, v3, and v8 are observed and the other variables are missing, for this observation you should return (v1 + v3 + v8) / 3. Use rowMeans() with care.


In a hypothetical dataset you have variables male (respondent’s gender, 0 = female and 1 = male), feduc (father’s education), and meduc (mother’s education). You want to create a variable ssedu that represents the level of education of the same-sex parent, i.e., for men the father and for women the mother. Provide code, and discuss what would happen if any of the three variables are missing.

1. Describing and imputing a single variable

title: Using functions
text: In this part you will learn about the use of functions (such as “take the square root”, “taking a substring of a string”, or “draw a random number” — the computer version of “flipping coins” — to accomplish various tasks in constructing or modifying variables. Functions may be embedded in arithmetic expressions, and they may also be composed. For instance, we may take the logarithm of a random variate with a uniform distribution on [0, 1]. We present the information, mostly in the context of assignments, under a number of headers:

title: Using functions
text:
Examples
Absolute difference dage of the age of husband (hage) and wife (wage):

data <- data |>   
  mutate(dage = abs(wage - hage)) 

Equivalent, using if_else():

data <- data |>   
  mutate(dage = if_else(wage > hage, wage - hage, hage - wage)) 

The natural logarithm of 1 + wagerate. Note that log(x) is missing for x <= 0.

data <- data |>   
  mutate(lnwage = log(1 + wagerate)) 

The maximum wage rate of the husband (hwage) and wife (wwage):

data <- data |>   
  mutate(maxwage = pmax(hwage, wwage)) 
# pmax stands for "parallel max". It compares the given columns for each row and
# returns the maximum value for *each row*. 

Income chopped at 100000:

data <- data |>   
  mutate(rinc = pmin(inc, 100000)) 

Length, number of characters, in the string variable cityname:

data <- data |>   
  mutate(nch = str_length(cityname)) 
# or nchar(cityname)

Display the number of full weeks in a year. The R Console can be used as an interactive calculator.

floor(365 / 7) 

Embellish unrounded output.

paste("number of full weeks in year =", round(365 / 7, 2)) 


Numeric functions

The following functions in R are important for the creation of new variables or the modification of existing variables. Make sure that you understand the functions. If you are uncertain, think of examples, and verify. In particular, check how to access the help pages for their definitions. Be sure to understand that these functions exist, roughly what they are good for, and how to find the details at the moment you really want to use them.




R
Description




sqrt(x)
square-root of x


abs(x)
the absolute value of x


pmin(x, y)
the minimum of x and y


pmax(x, y, z)
the maximum of x, y, and z


round(x)
x rounded to nearest integer


floor(x)
x rounded down


ceiling(x)
x rounded up


x %% y
remainder after dividing x by y


exp(x)
the exponential function


log(x)
the natural logarithm


log10(x)
the logarithm to the base 10



Functions and other operations may be mixed. For instance, you may write:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(lp = (log(p) / log(1 - p)) - 4) 
Functions may also be nested, or composed. For instance:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(fx = log(1 + exp(x))) 
Use parentheses if you are unsure about the priority of operators. What comes first, division or subtraction? Many inexperienced users will not remember (it is division). We recommend using parentheses rather than relying on your memory.
For each of these functions, what do you think will happen if the argument, or any of the arguments, is missing? Under what other conditions can each of these functions return a missing value? Experiment, or read the help pages.
A warning about round(): R rounds halves to the nearest even number, so round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4. See:

round(c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5))

[1] 0 2 2 4 4



Check the meaning of the following mathematical R functions.








R
Description




x %in% c(a, b, c, ...)
logical: x equals a, or b, or c, …


between(x, a, b)
logical: x ≥ a and x ≤ b


if_else(x, y, z)
if x, then y else z


case_when()
recode values using multiple conditions


cut(x, breaks)
recode a continuous variable into intervals





String functions
In R, string manipulation is commonly performed using functions from the stringr package, which is part of the tidyverse. Make sure that you understand the purpose of the following functions. If you are uncertain, think of examples and verify them.



R
Description




str_length(s)
length of string


str_to_lower(s)
convert string s to lowercase


str_to_upper(s)
convert string s to uppercase


str_detect(s, t)
test whether string t occurs in string s


str_locate(s, t)
position of string t in string s


str_sub(s, n, m)
substring of s from position n to m


str_trim(s)
drops leading and trailing blanks from s


as.numeric(s)
convert string s to a number


as.character(x)
convert object x to a string



As a more demanding task, split a string variable str into the first word (w1) and the remainder of the string (rest), where the first word is defined as all characters before first space.
data <- data |>   
  mutate(     
    first_space = str_locate(str, " ")[, 1],     
    w1   = str_sub(str, end = first_space-1),     
    rest = str_sub(str, start = first_space)  
  ) 
Does this code yield correct results if str has leading spaces? What if it has no spaces? Can you fix it? Can you think of a way to extract the second word?
For more complex operations with strings, it is useful to know the basics of regular expressions, which we do not cover in this course.
The functions as.numeric() and as.character() convert between strings and numeric values. When as.numeric() cannot interpret a string as a number, it returns NA.
In the assignments below you will apply string functions to manipulate dates and name-address information.


Other functions in R
There are plenty of other types of R functions. We do not expect you to remember all details of these or any of the other functions you encounter here, just that you get an understanding of the kinds of tasks that may be accomplished with functions, and how to access information about them when needed.

Random number generation

runif(1) draws a random number from the uniform distribution (by default, between 0 and 1). Each time you invoke runif(), the function returns a different value.
sample(1:5, 1) returns 1, 2, …, 5 each with the same probability.
rbinom(1, 1, 0.75) generates a 1 with probability 0.75, and a 0 with probability 0.25. rbinom(1, 1, 0.5) generates 0 and 1 with equal probability. (Check by generating a large number of random numbers — change argument n — and checking how many 1s and 0s were produced)
rnorm(1, 1.3, 2.5) generates a random number from a normal distribution with mean = 1.3 and standard deviation = 2.5.

For instance, to randomly select each observation in the data with probability 0.5:
data |>   
  mutate(selected = rbinom(n(), 1, 0.5)) |>
  filter(selected == 1) 
See ?Distributions for additional random number generators.


Missing value handling
The function is.na() returns TRUE if a value is missing and FALSE otherwise.
For instance, to select all observations that are not missing on the variables age, medu, and gender:
data |>   
  mutate(hasmiss = is.na(age) | is.na(medu) | is.na(gender)) |> 
  filter(!hasmiss) 

# Or equivalently 
data |>   
  mutate(notmiss = !is.na(age) & !is.na(medu) & !is.na(gender)) |> 
  filter(notmiss) 

# As always with R, other solutions are possible


Miscellaneous

row_number() returns the observation sequence number, that is, 1 in the first observation, 2 in the second observation, etc. One common application is to generate a case identifier:

data <- data |>   
  mutate(respnr = row_number()) 

n() returns the number of observations. Within .by or group_by(), it returns the number of observations in the group.

To create a variable with number of respondents in each household, indexed by hrespnr:
data |>   
  mutate(n_residents = n(), .by = hrespnr)

title: Using functions
text:
Assignments

Use sbs399.dta. We focus on the variable hrinc (hourly income).


What is the value of the mean and median of the untransformed variable?
For each of the following transformations, find the mean and the median: exp(hrinc), hrinc*hrinc, sqrt(hrinc), log(hrinc), hrinc (i.e., untransformed, identity), 1/sqrt(hrinc), 1/hrinc, and 1/(hrinc*hrinc).
For which transformation, including the no-transformation, is the variable most symmetrically distributed? You may gauge the symmetry of a distribution by its skewness. Recall: a positive skewness indicates a distribution tilted to the left, a negative skewness indicates a distribution tilted to the right. Compute the skewness using the function skewness() from the package parameters.


We focus on the variable hrinc in the original sbs399 data again. The values are decimal numbers such as 3.5. Generate transformations of this variable using functions:


round hrinc to the nearest integer (so any value between 3.5 and 4.5 should be rounded to 4);
round the variable down (so any value between 3 and 4 is rounded to 3);
round the variable up (so any value between 3 and 4 is rounded to 4);
round in multiples of 10 (so any value between 5 and 15 is rounded to 10);
clip to the range [10,50], i.e., values below 10 are set to 10; values above 50 are set to 50; values between 10 and 50 are returned unchanged. Check the range (min and max) of the clipped variable.
Inspect the first 10 values of the original variable and the above transformations.


The dataset sbs399 contains the educational level of the father and mother of respondents (feduc and meduc respectively). We define the educational resources of the parents (peduc) as the maximum of the educational levels of the parents. Give code to create peduc. Do you think that this conceptualization is also appropriate if education is seen as a proxy for attitudes?
Now use the home_work dataset, which includes 3 cases only. You want to compute the geographic distance d(h,w) between a subject’s home address and a subject’s work address. The data contain the geographic coordinates (home_x, home_y) and (work_x, work_y) of the home and work location, expressed as east-west and north-south distances from a reference point in the Netherlands, in units of 1 km, rounded. Give R code that computes the distance d between home and work, assuming a flat earth. Recall that by Pythagoras’ theorem

\[d(h,w) = \sqrt{(home_x - work_x)^2 + (home_y - work_y)^2}\]
(Did you dream of ever using this in the social sciences?) Round the distance in meaningful units, as locations are rounded in 1 km units, it does not make sense that distance is expressed in a finer unit, say meters.1

Use the dataset hin95_birthdates.


This dataset contains the respondent’s birth date rbirth, a numeric variable recording the birth dates in the format ddmmyy. Note that the number has 5 digits if dd < 10, and 6 digits otherwise. Construct three variables d_rbirth, m_rbirth, and y_rbirth with the day, month, and year in which the respondent was born. Use the functions %% and floor().
List the first twenty observations to verify your variable construction.
To check your work, you may actually reconstruct the original coding from the three variables, and verify that the reconstructed variable matches the original variable.


The file hin95_birthdates contains the respondent’s birth date as a string variable rbirth_str in the format "ddmmyy". The string is of length 5 if dd < 10, and of length 6 otherwise. Use string functions to construct three variables with the day, month, and year in which the respondent was born.
The dataset hin95_naw contains name, address, and city information. This is a random selection of address information that we purchased from the Dutch mail agency for the “Households in the Netherlands in 1995” project. In this assignment we do some manipulations of this dataset with address information.


The string variable postcode contains postcodes in the Dutch format 1234 AB. Construct a new numeric variable npcode that contains the numeric part. Thus, from 1234 AB we want to extract the part 1234. This is useful to merge information that is being organized with respect to geographic information, e.g., for contextual analyses. First take the substring of the first initial characters, i.e., convert 1234 AB to a string 1234. Then convert this string to a number, thus the string 1234 to the number 1234. Be sure to understand the difference. What is the mean value of npcode? How do you interpret this number?

title: Using functions
text:
Footnotes


For the interested reader: How do you obtain such location information yourself? If the dataset contains address information or postal codes, it is possible to use geocoding tools to obtain geolocations. Such tools can add new variables with cleaned address information and geographic coordinates. Using these geolocations you may compute, as explained above, the distance as the crow flies assuming a flat earth. If you pedantically want to account for the curvature of the earth, R also has packages that compute distances using geographic coordinates on the surface of the earth. More advanced students can even take into account that due to its spinning, the earth has to a high degree of accuracy an ellipsoid shape, not a ball shape. Then again, for a small country as the Netherlands such fine points are fully immaterial. Additional tools and packages provide access to other map services, such as the travel distance and travel time between two locations, distinguishing travel by car, by public transportation, by bike, and walking. One can also add variables with facilities, e.g., the number of schools within a 2 km radius around a location.↩︎

title: Restructuring data
text:
We may present panel data, data on people indicated by id, for different years indicated by year, in long format. To keep things simple, suppose for now that we only measured one time-varying variable, income inc, alongside the time-constant variable male:
or in wide format:
Be sure that you understand that these two datasets contain the same information, but only represent the information in a different way. One can translate one form into the other form. The variable inc is said to be time-varying, while male is time-constant.
In this part you practice the R functions that restructure data between long format and wide format. You need to learn about this because your data may be in one format, while the data management or statistical method you want to use requires the data to be in the other format.
For instance, multilevel analysis typically requires data to be in long format, e.g., measurements at different time points are stored in different rows, while structural equation modeling often requires wide data, e.g., measurements stored in different variables. In SaSR7 you will learn about these statistical methods. For now, we only introduce how to get the data into the correct format.

title: Restructuring data
text:
R
You should read about the following R functions:



Function
Description




pivot_longer()
Convert data from wide to long format


pivot_wider()
Convert data from long to wide format



Examples:

A single time-varying variable
Restructure long to wide. Every id becomes one row, and the values of year become new column names, prefixed with inc_:

data_wide <- data_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(id, male),
    names_from = year,
    names_prefix = "inc_",
    values_from = inc
  )

Restructure wide to long. The reverse operation recovers year from the column names, and inc from the values stored in those columns:

data_long <- data_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(id, male),
    names_prefix = "inc_",
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "inc"
  )

Things get a little more involved when more than one variable is time-varying, for instance if we also measure a person’s status stat every year:

Now a single column name, e.g. inc_2000, has to be split into two pieces of information: which variable (inc or stat) and which year (2000). pivot_wider() handles this by pivoting on more than one variable at once:

data_wide <- data_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(id, male),
    names_from = year,
    values_from = c(inc, stat)
  )

Going back to long format, we tell pivot_longer() that one part of the name (.value) becomes the new variable name, inc or stat, and the other part becomes the value of year:

data_long <- data_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(id, male),
    names_sep = "_",
    names_to = c(".value", "year")
  )

Note that pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() expect that variable names follow a consistent naming convention. In the examples above, the variables are named using a prefix, inc and stat, followed by a year, 2000, 2001, and 2002, corresponding to the level of an index variable, here the year in which income and status were measured, and names_sep = "_" is enough to tell R where the prefix ends and the year begins. If variables are not named consistently, you may need to rename them before restructuring the data.
Sometimes a single separator is not enough, for example when a name mixes a prefix, a single-letter sex code, and a two-digit wave without any separator at all, like inc_m01 or lit_f02. In such cases names_sep cannot locate the boundaries, and pivot_longer()/pivot_wider() instead need a regular expression (via the names_pattern argument) to describe the naming pattern. Regular expressions are a powerful but separate topic that we do not cover in this course; for now, it is enough to know that they exist for naming conventions that names_sep cannot handle.

title: Restructuring data
text:
Assignments

1. Longitudinal data in long and wide format
The dataset gpa2long.dta contains longitudinal data, taken from the book on multilevel analysis that we use in SaSR7, in long format.

student student identifier
occas measurement occasion, 0 = year 1 semester 1, 1 = year 1 semester 2, 2 = year 2 semester 1, 3 = year 2 semester 2, …
sex 0 = male, 1 = female
gpa grade-point average
job paid work hours per week
highgpa high school GPA
admitted admitted to university, 0 = no, 1 = yes, or missing


Which variables are time-constant and which are time-varying?
How many observations are there for student 1 and student 2?
Use pivot_wider() to convert the data to wide format using occas as the measurement occasion. Save it as a new object called gpa2wide.
Which new variables are created?
How many observations does the wide dataset contain?
Convince yourself that information was preserved across the restructuring and that only the representation of the information changed.
Use pivot_longer() to convert gpa2wide it back to long format.



2. Sex-specific country indicators
In this assignment, we use the World95 dataset. This dataset contains information for 109 countries. One observation corresponds to one country.
Some variables are sex-specific, e.g., the life expectancy for men and women (lifeexpm and lifeexpf respectively) and the literacy rates of men and women (lit_male and lit_fema respectively). Other variables, e.g., populatn and density, are not sex-specific.
We want to create a dataset in which each country is represented by two observations, one describing the men and one describing the women of that country.
A new dummy variable female should describe whether a record pertains to women or men.
Thus, a new dataset has to be constructed with 2 × 109 = 218 observations, with at least the following variables:

country
female
population
density
lifeexp
lit

where population and density do not vary with gender, while lifeexp and lit do.

Which variables are gender-specific and which are not?
Rename variables if necessary so that they follow a consistent naming convention.
Use pivot_longer() to create the desired dataset.
Create a variable female.
Verify that the resulting dataset contains 218 observations and 109 countries.



3. Multilevel data in four formats
The synthetic dataset level4.dta contains multilevel data on three sex-role attitude measurements over time, 2002, 2004, and 2006, for both spouses of heterosexual couples.

hhid household id
iid individual id
urban urbanized
male
edu highest completed education, 1 to 10
year
att1 family value: man natural breadwinner
att2 family value: women are better with children
att3 family value: men and women equal decision makers

We say that the dataset level4 is in long-long-long-wide format for the key variables hhid, iid, year, and (not-existing) item. The first term long refers to households, and reflects that households are stored in different observations identified by hhid. The second term long refers to individuals, and reflects that partners are stored as separate observations identified by iid; the variable hhid allows linking people who form a couple. The third long refers to time: measurements at different time points are stored in different observations, with time indicated by the variable year. The final term wide specifies that the repeated attitude measurements are stored in different variables within an observation, not as different observations.
Make sure that you understand the data well.

Use pivot_longer() to convert the data from long-long-long-wide to long-long-long-long format, i.e., the items are stored in different observations rather than in different variables indexed by a new variable item.
Use pivot_wider() to convert the data from the original long-long-long-wide format to long-long-wide-wide format. Explain what an observation in this dataset represents.
Use pivot_wider() to convert the data from the original long-long-long-wide format to long-wide-wide-wide format, identifying individuals within households by male rather than by iid. What happens if you identify people within households by iid? Is using male as a person-within-household identifier correct if the data include same-sex households?

Which variables are time-constant and which are time-varying? You can answer this by thinking about the meaning of the variables and looking informally at the data.

student: a person identifier, so should be time-constant
occas: the time index, so it is by definition time-varying
sex: time-constant
gpa: time-varying, can change each semester
job: time-varying: working hours change between semesters
highgpa: time-constant, as it’s the final high school GPA
admitted: time-constant, there is a single admission decision per student

But to be sure we can check the number of distinct values of each variable within each student. If a variable has more than one distinct value for a student, it is time-varying; if it has only one distinct value, it is time-constant.

  mutate(
    n_occas    = n_distinct(occas),
    n_sex      = n_distinct(sex),
    n_gpa      = n_distinct(gpa),
    n_job      = n_distinct(job),

# names_sep indicates that the names of the variables we want to make longer contain more than one piece of information, separated by "_" (job_0, gpa_3, etc).

Is male a correct person-within-household identifier? Only for heterosexual couples, which is what this synthetic dataset contains. In a same-sex household both partners share the same value of male, so the pair no longer identifies them uniquely. pivot_wider() wouldfind two values for one cell and return a list column with a warning about duplicate identifiers, rather than the intend two sets of columns.
One solution would be creating a gender-neutral unique identifier within each houseold (partner 1, partner 2), and use that instead:

level4 |>
  mutate(
    partner = dense_rank(iid),
    .by = hhid
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(hhid, urban),
    names_from = c(partner, year),
    values_from = c(att1, att2, att3, edu),

title: Aggregating data
text:
In this chapter you learn about the two related tasks:
To illustrate, consider the following toy dataset with 5 pupils with respondent identifier id, from 2 school classes identified by the variable class, recording the father’s education of the pupil in the variable fedu.
The dataset with class-level summary statistics should contain 2 cases, one for each class, with the mean of fedu in the respective classes, new variable mean_fedu, and the number of observations, new variable n, in each class.
The original individual-level dataset enriched with class-level summary statistics should read:
Thus, the variable mean_fedu records contextual, class-level, information; the mean education of the parents in a pupil’s class is treated as an individual attribute.

title: Aggregating data
text:
R
In this part you need to study the following R functions:



Function
Description




summarise()
Create a dataset with summary statistics


mutate()
Add new variables to the existing dataset


.by
Apply summarise() or mutate() within groups


n()
Count the number of observations in a group



We present a short code fragment to accomplish the data manipulation described in the preamble.
Add the mean of fedu by class as a variable:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    mean_fedu = mean(fedu, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = class
  )

Note that we could also have used the function group_by() to create a grouping structure, and then mutate() would have been applied within the groups. The .by argument is a convenient (and more recent) alternative that applies the operation separately within groups without permanently changing the grouping structure of the dataset. So the code below is a valid alternative to the code above:

data <- data |> 
  group_by(class) |>
  mutate(
    mean_fedu = mean(fedu, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

(Read more about group_by() and .by here.)
Add variable nclass: number of observations in each class:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    nclass = n(),
    .by = class
  )

Create a N = 2 contextual dataset with the N and mean of fedu, grouped by class:

class_data <- data |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_fedu = mean(fedu, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = class
  )

Make sure you understand the difference between mutate() and summarise(). The former enriches the individual-level dataset with class-level summary statistics, while the latter reduces the dataset to one row per group, thus creating a new dataset with class-level summary statistics.

title: Aggregating data
text:
Assignments

1. People nested within neighborhoods within cities
We consider a simple synthetic dataset ex_aggr.dta of people nested within neighborhoods nested within cities.

city city code
neighb neighborhood code
employ employment status, 1 = employed, 0 = unemployed
ethnic 1 = native Dutch; 2 = western immigrant; 3 = nonwestern immigrant


Create a separate dataset recording, for each city, the number of people, the fraction of unemployed and the ethnic composition, i.e., the frac8tions of native Dutch, western immigrants, and nonwestern immigrants.
Add variables to the original dataset with the percentages of unemployed and the ethnic composition of the neighborhood, i.e., the fractions, or percentages, of Dutch, western, and nonwestern people in the neighborhood. Consider how to also add the information aggregated at the city level.
Add a variable representing the percentage of ethnic ingroup in the neighborhood.
What is the average percentage of ethnic ingroup in the neighborhood for native Dutch, western immigrants, and nonwestern immigrants?



2. Education within couples
Use hin95_ext.dta. The dataset contains data on couples (married or cohabiting), as well as people living alone. The households are indicated by the identifier hrespnr. Keep only the couples, i.e., households with exactly two members. The variable educ records the level of education of the respondent.

Add a variable for the mean education of the household. Thus, this variable should have the same value for both partners.
Add a variable for the minimum education of the household. Add a variable for the maximum education of the household.
Add a variable recording the absolute difference of the levels of education of husband and wife.

title: Some programming features in R
text:
Objects allow you to abbreviate commands considerably, making code more readable, and improving consistency. For instance, we can define an object C with a set of variables to be used as controls in a series of models. Using an object ensures you use the same control variables everywhere; changing the controls in all models is accomplished by editing one line of code.

C <- c("sex", "age", "married")

title: Some programming features in R
Some programming features in R
text:
Writing your own functions
If you repeat the same block of code many times, it can be useful to write your own function. A function takes inputs, does something with them, and returns an output.

rob_regress <- function(formula, data) {

  lm(
    formula = formula,
    data = data
  )

}

This function is called rob_regress. It takes two inputs: a model formula and a dataset. Inside the function, lm() estimates a linear regression model.

rob_regress(
  inc ~ edu + age,
  data = data
)

This runs the function with income as the dependent variable and education and age as explanatory variables.

title: Simple linear regression
text:
Use the dataset anscombe. This built-in dataset contains four pairs of variables, (x1,y1), (x2,y2), (x3,y3), and (x4,y4).

Fit four separate bivariate regressions: y1 on x1, y2 on x2, y3 on x3, and y4 on x4. Compare the intercepts, slopes, standard errors, and \(R^2\) values of the four models. What do you notice?
Make a scatterplot with a fitted regression line for each of the four pairs. Inspect the four plots side by side (for example using patchwork or facet_wrap() after reshaping the data to long format).
What is your conclusion? Why is it not sufficient to only report regression coefficients and \(R^2\)?





Use the dataset state_crime. This dataset contains, for each U.S. state, the murder rate (murder) and a poverty score (poverty).

Make a scatterplot of murder against poverty, with state names (state) as labels. Which state stands out as an outlier?
Fit a regression of murder on poverty using all states. Report and interpret the intercept, the slope, and \(R^2\).
Refit the regression excluding the outlying state, without removing the observation from the dataset (use a filter() inside the data argument, or subset only for this call). Compare the intercept, slope, and \(R^2\) to the results in the previous question. What is the effect of this single observation on the results?




Use the dataset sbs399. We focus on the relation between age and hourly income hrinc.

Make a scatterplot of hrinc against age. Do you notice anything unusual in the data (for instance, in the distribution of hrinc)? Does the relationship look linear?
Fit a regression of hrinc on age. Interpret the intercept, the slope, and \(R^2\).
Compute the mean of hrinc separately for men and women (e.g. using group_by() and summarise(), or t.test()). What is the difference between the two means?
Fit a regression of hrinc on sex (a dummy variable). Compare the regression coefficient for sex to the difference in means found in the previous question. What do you conclude about the relation between a two-group t-test and a regression on a dummy variable?




Use the dataset sesam. We study the relation between a general IQ test score (peabody) and a post-test score (postnumb).

Make a scatterplot of postnumb against peabody. Does the relationship look linear, or does it look like it is increasing but at a decreasing rate?
Fit a linear regression of postnumb on peabody. Report and interpret the intercept, slope, and \(R^2\). Is the null hypothesis of no relation between peabody and postnumb rejected?
Create a dummy variable female from sex. Compare the mean postnumb of boys and girls using t.test(), and again using a regression of postnumb on female. Do the two approaches agree? Is there evidence that boys and girls differ, on average, on postnumb?

Scatterplots with fitted regression line:

ggplot(anscombe, aes(x = x1, y = y1)) +

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









All four plots combined, after reshaping to long format:

anscombe_long <- anscombe |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c(".value", "set"),
    names_pattern = "(x|y)(\\d)"
  )

anscombe_long |>
  slice(1:8)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  set       x     y
  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 1        10  8.04
2 2        10  9.14
3 3        10  7.46
4 4         8  6.58
5 1         8  6.95
6 2         8  8.14
7 3         8  6.77
8 4         8  5.76

# ".value" turns x and y into columns, the digit becomes the set number
# note that we pivot the raw anscombe data: adding a row number first would
# create a column that does not match the pattern


ggplot(anscombe_long, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ set) +
  labs(title = "Anscombe's quartet")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








# Results (coefficients, SEs, R-squared) for all four regressions are identical.
# From these results you might be tempted to conclude that the data look
# identical. But the four scatterplots look completely different:
# - Set 1: a roughly linear relationship, well described by the line.
# - Set 2: a clear curved (nonlinear) relationship; a line is not appropriate.
# - Set 3: a perfect linear relationship except for one outlier that pulls
#   the line away from the other points.
# - Set 4: no relationship at all except for one high-leverage point that
#   alone determines the slope.
# Conclusion: never rely on regression coefficients and R-squared alone,
# always inspect a scatterplot.




Crime and poverty

2. Spotting the outlier

ggplot(state_crime, aes(x = poverty, y = murder)) +
  geom_point()







ggplot(state_crime, aes(x = poverty, y = murder, label = state)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(nudge_y = 0.5, size = 3)







# The outlier is Washington DC, with an exceptionally high murder rate.


state_crime |>
  slice_max(murder, n = 5) |>
  select(state, poverty, murder)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  state poverty murder
  <chr>   <dbl>  <dbl>
1 DC       26.4   78.5
2 LA       26.4   20.3
3 MS       24.7   13.5
4 NY       16.4   13.3
5 CA       18.2   13.1

# the five highest murder rates, to confirm how far DC stands apart



3. Regression using all states

fit_crime <- lm(murder ~ poverty, data = state_crime)
summary(fit_crime)


Call:
lm(formula = murder ~ poverty, data = state_crime)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-12.333  -4.177  -0.875   1.569  53.710 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -10.1364     4.1206  -2.460   0.0175 *  
poverty       1.3230     0.2754   4.804 1.51e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 8.926 on 49 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3202,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3063 
F-statistic: 23.08 on 1 and 49 DF,  p-value: 1.508e-05

# E(murder) = -10.14 + 1.32 poverty       (SE = 0.28)
#
# A 1 unit increase in the poverty scale yields a predicted increase of
# 1.32 units in the murder rate. R-squared = 0.32: 32% of the variance
# in murder rate is explained by the poverty rate.


confint(fit_crime)

                  2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) -18.4170837 -1.855707
poverty       0.7695805  1.876339

# a confidence interval for the slope, to compare with the next model

Note that the intercept is negative, which would mean a negative murder rate at a poverty score of 0. That is not a defect of the model: a poverty score of 0 lies outside the range of the data, so the intercept has no substantive interpretation here.

range(state_crime$poverty)

[1]  8.0 26.4

# the observed range of poverty; the intercept extrapolates far below it



4. Regression excluding the outlier

fit_crime_no_dc <- lm(murder ~ poverty, data = state_crime |> filter(state != "DC"))
summary(fit_crime_no_dc)


Call:
lm(formula = murder ~ poverty, data = filter(state_crime, state != 
    "DC"))

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-5.2134 -2.2472 -0.3956  2.2659  7.8896 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  -0.8567     1.5278  -0.561    0.578    
poverty       0.5842     0.1043   5.600 1.02e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 3.131 on 48 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3952,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3826 
F-statistic: 31.36 on 1 and 48 DF,  p-value: 1.017e-06

# E(murder) = -0.86 + 0.58 poverty        (SE = 0.10)
#
# A 1 unit increase in the poverty scale now gives a predicted increase
# of only 0.58 units in the murder rate, about half the earlier estimate.
# R-squared = 0.40: 40% of the variance in murder rate is now explained
# by the poverty rate. A single unusual observation (DC) had a
# substantial effect on the slope, its standard error, and R-squared.


bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "all states", intercept = coef(fit_crime)[1], slope = coef(fit_crime)[2],
         r_squared = summary(fit_crime)$r.squared),
  tibble(model = "without DC", intercept = coef(fit_crime_no_dc)[1], slope = coef(fit_crime_no_dc)[2],
         r_squared = summary(fit_crime_no_dc)$r.squared)
)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  model      intercept slope r_squared
  <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 all states   -10.1   1.32      0.320
2 without DC    -0.857 0.584     0.395

# the two models side by side


ggplot(state_crime, aes(x = poverty, y = murder)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = state_crime |> filter(state != "DC"),
    method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed"
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








# solid line: all states; dashed line: excluding DC
# one observation visibly rotates the fitted line

Note that dropping DC raises \(R^2\) even though the fit is now based on less extreme data. \(R^2\) is a ratio, and DC inflated both the explained and the total variance; removing it changes the two by different amounts. This is a good reason not to read \(R^2\) as a measure of how “good” a model is in any absolute sense.



Income and age

5. Scatterplot of income against age

ggplot(sbs399, aes(x = age, y = hrinc)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 1381 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








# We expect a positive relation between age and hourly income.
# A number of observations have hrinc equal to exactly 100. It is unclear
# whether this reflects missing values or values top-coded at 100 -- this
# should be checked. These observations may be outliers in Y-space.
# The relation may not be strictly linear; possibly quadratic.

Check the suspicion about the value 100 before doing anything else.

sbs399 |>
  count(hrinc) |>
  slice_max(hrinc, n = 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  hrinc     n
  <dbl> <int>
1 100       8
2  92.3     1
3  90       1
4  86.6     1
5  73.1     1

# a spike at exactly 100 would confirm top-coding or a missing value code


sum(sbs399$hrinc == 100, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 8

# how many observations sit exactly at 100



6. Regression of income on age

fit_age <- lm(hrinc ~ age, data = sbs399)
summary(fit_age)


Call:
lm(formula = hrinc ~ age, data = sbs399)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-20.503  -4.030  -1.474   1.737  83.604 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  8.02366    0.89163   8.999   <2e-16 ***
age          0.28871    0.02472  11.681   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.142 on 1967 degrees of freedom
  (1381 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.06487,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.06439 
F-statistic: 136.4 on 1 and 1967 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

# E(hrinc) = 8.02 + 0.29 age               (SE = 0.03)
#
# R-squared = 0.065. If age increases by 1 year, hourly income
# significantly rises by 0.29 EUR. Age explains 6.5% of the variance
# in income.

The intercept of 8.02 is the predicted income at age 0, which is meaningless in itself: nobody in the data is anywhere near that age.

range(sbs399$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 18 79

# centring age would give the intercept a usable interpretation


lm(hrinc ~ I(age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)), data = sbs399) |>
  coef()

                     (Intercept) I(age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) 
                      18.9177742                        0.2887148 

# after centring, the intercept is the predicted income at the mean age
# the slope is unchanged



7. Mean income for men and women

table(sbs399$sex, useNA = "ifany")


   0    1 
1699 1651 

# sex = 0 for men and sex = 1 for women


sbs399 |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(mean_hrinc = mean(hrinc, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex       mean_hrinc
  <dbl+lbl>      <dbl>
1 0 [man]         19.6
2 1 [woman]       16.2

t.test(hrinc ~ sex, data = sbs399)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hrinc by sex
t = 8.1499, df = 1868.4, p-value = 6.596e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 0 and group 1 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.591711 4.234369
sample estimates:
mean in group 0 mean in group 1 
       19.59728        16.18424 

# E(hrinc) for men = 19.60; E(hrinc) for women = 16.18
# Women have 3.42 EUR lower income than men.



8. Regression on a dummy variable

fit_sex <- lm(hrinc ~ sex, data = sbs399)
summary(fit_sex)


Call:
lm(formula = hrinc ~ sex, data = sbs399)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-19.497  -4.684  -1.784   1.716  83.816 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  19.5973     0.2757  71.073  < 2e-16 ***
sex          -3.4130     0.4244  -8.041 1.52e-15 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.302 on 1967 degrees of freedom
  (1381 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.03183,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.03134 
F-statistic: 64.66 on 1 and 1967 DF,  p-value: 1.519e-15

# The regression coefficient for sex = -3.41, which is the difference
# in expected hourly income between men and women -- the same result
# as the independent-samples t-test.


coef(fit_sex)

(Intercept)         sex 
   19.59728    -3.41304 

# the intercept is the mean of the reference group (sex = 0, men)
# the slope is the difference between the two group means


t.test(hrinc ~ sex, data = sbs399, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  hrinc by sex
t = 8.0413, df = 1967, p-value = 1.519e-15
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 0 and group 1 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.580646 4.245434
sample estimates:
mean in group 0 mean in group 1 
       19.59728        16.18424 

# the default t.test() does NOT assume equal variances, while lm() does
# with var.equal = TRUE the t-value and p-value match the regression exactly

A regression on a single dummy variable and an independent samples t-test are the same procedure, provided both assume equal variances. The regression formulation is more general: it extends to several predictors, whereas the t-test does not.



Nonlinearity

9. Scatterplot of postnumb against peabody

ggplot(sesam, aes(x = peabody, y = postnumb)) +
  geom_point()







# The relation looks nonlinear: it is increasing, but decreasingly so.
# A quadratic transformation of peabody might help.


ggplot(sesam, aes(x = peabody, y = postnumb)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








# the straight line and a smoother in one plot
# where the dashed curve bends away from the line, a linear model misfits



10. Linear regression of postnumb on peabody

fit_peabody <- lm(postnumb ~ peabody, data = sesam)
summary(fit_peabody)


Call:
lm(formula = postnumb ~ peabody, data = sesam)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-27.7455  -7.7933  -0.3047   7.7511  28.1208 

Coefficients:

A significant slope does not mean the linear model is appropriate. It only means a straight line fits better than a horizontal one.

Multiple R-squared:  0.2827,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2767 
F-statistic:  46.7 on 2 and 237 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

# if the quadratic term is significant, the relation is indeed curved
# compare the R-squared of the two models



11. Comparing boys and girls

table(sesam$sex, useNA = "ifany")


  1   2 
115 125 

# check the coding before constructing the dummy


sesam <- sesam |>
  mutate(female = sex - 1)

 -3.293537  3.252494

summary(fit_female)

-30.064 -11.043  -1.044  11.936  23.956

title: Binary logistic regression
text:
Use the dataset unemploy. Construct the outcome work, coded 1 if studytim (the unemployment spell length) is less than 53 (weeks), and 0 otherwise. Human capital is captured by edu (education), age, and exp (number of previous unemployment spells).


Fit a linear probability model of work on age, edu, and exp. Interpret each coefficient in terms of percentage-point changes in the probability of re-employment.



Refit the same model with heteroskedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors. Compare the coefficients and standard errors to the previous model. Are the substantive conclusions affected?



Obtain the predicted probabilities from the linear probability model. Count how many predicted probabilities fall outside the range 0 to 1. What does this tell you about the linear probability model in this particular dataset, and about the model in general?



Fit a logistic regression of work on age, edu, and exp. Interpret each coefficient in terms of log odds.



Exponentiate the coefficients from the previous model to obtain odds ratios. Interpret each odds ratio as a percentage change in the odds of re-employment. Why is the odds ratio interpretation valid for every subject, regardless of the specific values of the predictors, unlike a marginal effect?



Compute the average marginal effects for all predictors in the logistic model, on the probability scale. Compare these effects, and the substantive conclusions they imply, to the coefficients of the linear probability model from question 1.



Compute the marginal effect of age for a person with the lowest education level (edu = 1) and the largest number of prior unemployment spells (exp = 3). Interpret this effect.



Compute the marginal effect of age at the means of edu and exp. Compare this to the average marginal effect of age found in question 6. Why can these two values differ?



Fit a logistic regression of work on age, edu, and exp (human capital only), and a second model that adds three measures of social capital: scweak, scmedium, and scstrong. Test, using both a Wald test and a likelihood ratio test, whether social capital as a set significantly contributes to explaining re-employment, controlling for human capital. Do the two tests agree?



Using the full model from the previous question, test whether the three forms of social capital (scweak, scmedium, scstrong) have equal effects on re-employment. What do you conclude?



Fit a probit regression of work on age, edu, and exp. Compare the coefficients to the logistic regression from question 4. Are the substantive conclusions the same, even though the coefficients themselves are not directly comparable in size?

F-statistic: 10.89 on 3 and 238 DF,  p-value: 9.97e-07

# If age increases by one year, the probability of re-employment
# significantly decreases by 3.25 percentage points.
# If education increases, the probability of re-employment significantly
# increases by 5.6 percentage points per unit of education.
# If the number of previous unemployment spells (exp) is higher, the
# probability of re-employment does not decrease significantly at the
# 5% level, but does decrease significantly at the 7.7% level (by about
# 4.8 percentage points per additional spell).



2. Robust standard errors

coeftest(fit_lpm, vcov = vcovHC(fit_lpm, type = "HC1"))


t test of coefficients:

              Estimate Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  1.9923848  0.3286256  6.0628 5.208e-09 ***
age         -0.0325075  0.0065741 -4.9448 1.440e-06 ***
edu          0.0556019  0.0249057  2.2325   0.02651 *  
exp         -0.0476368  0.0269259 -1.7692   0.07814 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# The coefficients are exactly the same as in the OLS model; only the
# standard errors change slightly. The substantive conclusions are
# robust to this correction.



3. Predicted probabilities outside 0 and 1

unemploy <- unemploy |>
  mutate(prob_lpm = predict(fit_lpm))

unemploy |>
  summarise(n_out_of_range = sum(prob_lpm < 0 | prob_lpm > 1))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  n_out_of_range
           <int>
1              0

# None of the observations have predicted probabilities outside the
# range 0 to 1. In practice, this is very often the case, even though
# the linear probability model does not guarantee it in general.



4. Logistic regression: log odds

fit_logit <- glm(work ~ age + edu + exp, data = unemploy, family = binomial)
summary(fit_logit)


Call:
glm(formula = work ~ age + edu + exp, family = binomial, data = unemploy)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  6.55463    1.54276   4.249 2.15e-05 ***
age         -0.14314    0.03131  -4.572 4.84e-06 ***
edu          0.25873    0.12040   2.149   0.0316 *  
exp         -0.21646    0.12099  -1.789   0.0736 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 335.22  on 241  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 304.44  on 238  degrees of freedom
AIC: 312.44

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

# If age increases by one year, the log odds of re-employment
# significantly go down by 0.143.
# If education increases, the log odds of re-employment significantly
# increase by 0.259.
# If the number of previous unemployment spells is higher, the log odds
# of re-employment do not decrease significantly at the 5% level, but do
# decrease significantly at the 7.4% level (by 0.216).



5. Odds ratios

exp(coef(fit_logit))

(Intercept)         age         edu         exp 
702.4906694   0.8666365   1.2952779   0.8053685 

# The odds of getting a job within a year (the probability of getting a
# job divided by the probability of not getting a job) change by
# (exp(b) - 1) * 100% for a one-unit increase in x:
#   - the odds increase by (exp(0.259) - 1) * 100 = 29.5% for one unit
#     of education
#   - the odds change by (exp(-0.143) - 1) * 100 = -13.3%, i.e. decrease
#     by 13.3%, for each year older
#   - the odds decrease by about 19.5% for each previous unemployment
#     spell (exp(-0.216))
#
# The advantage of the odds ratio interpretation is that it applies
# exactly for every subject, irrespective of the value of the focal
# variable and of the values of the other predictors -- unlike a
# marginal effect, which depends on the specific values of all
# predictors.



6. Average marginal effects

avg_slopes(fit_logit)


 Term Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S    2.5 %   97.5 %
  age  -0.0314    0.00566 -5.55   <0.001 25.0 -0.04251 -0.02031
  edu   0.0568    0.02551  2.23   0.0260  5.3  0.00678  0.10678
  exp  -0.0475    0.02591 -1.83   0.0668  3.9 -0.09829  0.00329

Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX

# variable | coefficient (log odds) |  odds ratio | average marginal effect
# ---------+-------------------------+-------------+--------------------------
#      age |          -0.143         |    0.867    |        -0.031
#      edu |           0.259         |    1.295    |         0.057
#      exp |          -0.216         |    0.805    |        -0.0475
#
# With each year of age, the probability of re-employment decreases on
# average by about 3.1 percentage points. The effects of the other
# predictors follow similarly. These average marginal effects are very
# close to the coefficients of the linear probability model in question
# 1. In practice, this is very often the case.



7. Marginal effect at chosen values

slopes(fit_logit, variables = "age", newdata = datagrid(edu = 1, exp = 3))


 edu exp Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 %  97.5 %
   1   3  -0.0318    0.00742 -4.29   <0.001 15.8 -0.0463 -0.0173

Term: age
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX

# For the lowest educated people with the largest number of prior
# unemployment spells, a one-year increase in age is associated with a
# significant decrease in the probability of re-employment of about
# 3.0 percentage points.



8. Marginal effect at the means

slopes(fit_logit, variables = "age", newdata = "mean")


 Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 %  97.5 %
  -0.0358    0.00783 -4.57   <0.001 17.7 -0.0511 -0.0204

Term: age
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX

# For a person with average education and an average number of prior
# unemployment spells, a one-year increase in age is associated with a
# significant decrease in the probability of re-employment of about
# 3.6 percentage points. This differs from the average marginal effect
# in question 6, because there we averaged the marginal effect over all
# observed combinations of education and prior unemployment spells,
# rather than evaluating the effect once at the mean values of these
# predictors.



9. Does social capital contribute?

fit_hc <- glm(work ~ age + edu + exp, data = unemploy, family = binomial)
fit_hsc <- glm(work ~ age + edu + exp + scweak + scmedium + scstrong,
                data = unemploy, family = binomial)

# Wald test on relevance of social capital
linearHypothesis(fit_hsc, c("scweak = 0", "scmedium = 0", "scstrong = 0"))


Linear hypothesis test:
scweak = 0
scmedium = 0
scstrong = 0

Model 1: restricted model
Model 2: work ~ age + edu + exp + scweak + scmedium + scstrong

  Res.Df Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)  
1    238                       
2    235  3 7.3409    0.06179 .
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Likelihood ratio test on relevance of social capital
lrtest(fit_hc, fit_hsc)

Likelihood ratio test

Model 1: work ~ age + edu + exp
Model 2: work ~ age + edu + exp + scweak + scmedium + scstrong
  #Df  LogLik Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)  
1   4 -152.22                       
2   7 -148.40  3 7.6431    0.05399 .
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# We find weak evidence that social capital affects re-employment,
# controlling for human capital (LR chi2(3) = 7.6, p = 0.053). The Wald
# test gives a similar conclusion.



10. Are the three forms of social capital equal?

linearHypothesis(fit_hsc, c("scweak = scmedium", "scmedium = scstrong"))


Linear hypothesis test:
scweak - scmedium = 0
scmedium - scstrong = 0

Model 1: restricted model
Model 2: work ~ age + edu + exp + scweak + scmedium + scstrong

  Res.Df Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)  
1    237                       
2    235  2 6.1095    0.04713 *
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# We can reject the null hypothesis that, controlling for human capital,
# the three forms of social capital affect re-employment to the same
# degree (chi2(2) = 6.11, p = 0.047).



11. Logit versus probit

fit_probit <- glm(work ~ age + edu + exp, data = unemploy, family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(fit_probit)


Call:
glm(formula = work ~ age + edu + exp, family = binomial(link = "probit"), 
    data = unemploy)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  3.98340    0.92838   4.291 1.78e-05 ***
age         -0.08693    0.01875  -4.636 3.55e-06 ***
edu          0.15507    0.07270   2.133   0.0329 *  
exp         -0.13167    0.07380  -1.784   0.0744 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 335.22  on 241  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 304.66  on 238  degrees of freedom
AIC: 312.66

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

# The probit coefficients are smaller in absolute size than the logit
# coefficients (as expected, since the two models are scaled
# differently), but the signs, significance, and substantive
# conclusions are the same. Indeed, conclusions from the linear
# probability model, the logit model, and the probit model are very
# often similar in practice, even though the models differ in their
# assumptions and in how coefficients are scaled.

title: Event history analysis
text:
Use the dataset hschool. The variables are: caseid (case identifier), time (time in months until school drop-out, or censoring), died (event indicator: 1 = dropped out, 0 = censored), sex (0 = male, 1 = female), grades (1 = high grades, 5 = low grades), parttime (1 = part-time student), mrg (month of marriage, coded as \(12 \times (\text{year} - 1980) + \text{month}\); 99 = never married), and stm (month of college entry, coded the same way).



How many students were married before entering college (i.e., mrg occurred before stm)?
How many students got married during college (i.e., mrg fell between stm and stm + time)?





We are interested in the effect of sex and grades on the time until school drop-out. Fit a linear regression of time on sex and grades, making sure you correctly restrict the sample to only those subjects for whom drop-out actually occurred. Interpret all coefficients, including the intercept — and note anything odd or hard to interpret about the intercept.





Fit a Cox proportional hazards model of drop-out on sex and grades. Interpret each coefficient (a) as an effect on the log hazard, and (b) as a hazard ratio.
Compare the statistical significance of sex and grades in the Cox model to their significance in the linear regression from question 3. Are the conclusions the same? If not, why is this not a contradiction?





Plot the hazard function, the cumulative hazard function, and the survival function implied by the Cox model.





Test the proportional hazards assumption for the Cox model of question 4. Does the assumption hold?





Construct a person-period file from hschool: one row per subject per month at risk, with an event indicator equal to 1 only in the month drop-out actually occurred (0 in all other months, including for censored subjects). Fit a discrete-time event history model using logistic regression of the event indicator on sex and grades. What do you conclude, and how does this compare to the conclusions from the Cox model?
