title: Event history analysis
text:
Answers
Make sure this file is in the same R Project as the data folder. Use relative file paths, not full paths to your computer.

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(haven)
library(survival)
library(survminer)

Loading required package: ggpubr

Attaching package: 'survminer'

The following object is masked from 'package:survival':

    myeloma

hschool <- read_dta("data/hschool.dta")

hschool <- hschool |>
  mutate(female = sex)


Data description

1. Married before entering college

hschool |>
  filter(mrg < stm) |>
  nrow()

[1] 4




2. Married during college

hschool |>
  filter(mrg >= stm, mrg <= stm + time) |>
  nrow()

[1] 10





Linear regression on duration

3. A linear regression on completed durations

fit_lm <- lm(time ~ sex + grades, data = hschool |> filter(died == 1))
summary(fit_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = time ~ sex + grades, data = filter(hschool, died == 
    1))

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-15.078  -9.379  -4.579   7.134  29.472 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 18.55328    3.13639   5.915 4.27e-08 ***
sex         -0.07509    2.39191  -0.031    0.975    
grades      -1.47489    0.96507  -1.528    0.129    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.03 on 104 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.02206,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.003258 
F-statistic: 1.173 on 2 and 104 DF,  p-value: 0.3134

# Females drop out about 0.075 months faster than males, but this is
# not significant.
# People with lower grades (higher values of grades, since 1 = high,
# 5 = low) drop out faster, but this is not significant either.
# Males (sex = 0) with the highest grades (grades = 0, which is outside
# the actual scale of 1-5 and should ideally be recentered) are
# predicted to drop out at 18.55 months. Because grades = 0 does not
# occur in the data, this intercept is not substantively meaningful as
# it stands.




Cox proportional hazards model

4. The Cox model

fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(time, died) ~ sex + grades, data = hschool)
summary(fit_cox)

Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(time, died) ~ sex + grades, data = hschool)

  n= 265, number of events= 107 

          coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z Pr(>|z|)    
sex    0.21833   1.24400  0.19851 1.100    0.271    
grades 0.33965   1.40446  0.08536 3.979 6.92e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

       exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
sex        1.244     0.8039     0.843     1.836
grades     1.404     0.7120     1.188     1.660

Concordance= 0.606  (se = 0.028 )
Likelihood ratio test= 16.06  on 2 df,   p=3e-04
Wald test            = 16.55  on 2 df,   p=3e-04
Score (logrank) test = 16.95  on 2 df,   p=2e-04

# Log hazard interpretation:
# Females have a 0.240 higher log hazard of dropping out than males (a
# shorter time to drop-out), but this is not significant.
# People with lower grades have a significantly higher log hazard of
# dropping out (a shorter time to drop-out).
#
# Hazard ratio interpretation (exp(coef), shown directly in the
# summary() output):
# Females have a 27% higher hazard of dropping out than males, but this
# is not significant.
# People with lower grades have a 39.73% significantly higher hazard of
# dropping out for each unit increase on the grades scale (i.e., each
# step toward lower grades).



5. Comparing the two models

# The significance of the predictors is not the same between the linear
# regression (question 3) and the Cox regression (question 4): grades is
# significant in the Cox model but not in the linear regression. This is
# not a contradiction. The linear regression restricts the sample to
# completed durations only and assumes normally distributed, constant-
# variance residuals on the raw time scale -- assumptions that are
# typically violated for duration data. The Cox model instead uses all
# subjects (including censored ones) and does not require these
# distributional assumptions, which is why it can detect an effect the
# linear model misses.


hschool |>
  count(died)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
   died     n
  <dbl> <int>
1     0   158
2     1   107

# how many cases the linear regression discards as censored




Plotting the process

6. Hazard, cumulative hazard, and survival

fit_surv <- survfit(fit_cox)

# Cumulative hazard
plot(fit_surv, fun = "cumhaz", xlab = "Time (months)", ylab = "Cumulative hazard")







# Survival function
plot(fit_surv, xlab = "Time (months)", ylab = "Survival probability")







# Using survminer for nicer plots, including an approximate hazard shape
# via the cumulative hazard and survival curves:
ggsurvplot(fit_surv, data = hschool, fun = "cumhaz")







ggsurvplot(fit_surv, data = hschool)







# Note: a smoothed hazard function itself (as opposed to the cumulative
# hazard) is not directly returned by survfit(); it can be approximated
# with a kernel-smoothed estimate, e.g. using the muhaz package, if a
# separate plot of the hazard function itself (rather than the
# cumulative hazard) is required.




Testing the proportional hazards assumption

7. The Schoenfeld residual test

cox.zph(fit_cox)

        chisq df    p
sex    0.0862  1 0.77
grades 0.7561  1 0.38
GLOBAL 0.8253  2 0.66

# The test does not reject the proportional hazards assumption at
# conventional significance levels: the proportional hazards assumption
# appears to hold for this model.




BONUS: discrete-time analysis

8. A person-period file and a discrete-time model

# Method 1: expand the data manually to one row per subject per month
person_period <- hschool |>
  dplyr::select(caseid, time, sex, grades, died) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(period = list(seq_len(time))) |>
  unnest(period) |>
  ungroup() |>
  rename(end_time = time) |>
  mutate(
    time = period,
    died = if_else(died == 1 & time != end_time, 0L, as.integer(died))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(caseid, time, end_time, sex, grades, died)

fit_discrete <- glm(died ~ sex + grades, data = person_period, family = binomial)
summary(fit_discrete)


Call:
glm(formula = died ~ sex + grades, family = binomial, data = person_period)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept) -5.28343    0.27359 -19.311  < 2e-16 ***
sex          0.26622    0.20145   1.321    0.186    
grades       0.35547    0.08689   4.091  4.3e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 1129.5  on 8085  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 1112.2  on 8083  degrees of freedom
AIC: 1118.2

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 7

# The discrete-time logistic model leads to the same substantive
# conclusion as the Cox model: grades significantly predicts drop-out
# (lower grades associated with higher risk of dropping out in a given
# month), while sex does not significantly predict drop-out. This
# confirms that the Cox model's conclusions are not an artifact of the
# continuous-time approach; a discrete-time formulation using ordinary
# logistic regression on the person-period file gives essentially the
# same answer.


nrow(hschool)

[1] 265

nrow(person_period)

[1] 8086

sum(person_period$died)

[1] 106

sum(hschool$died)

[1] 107

# one row per subject per month at risk; the number of events is
# unchanged, since each subject can drop out only once

title: Multinomial logistic regression
text:
Use the dataset hin95_voting.



Recode the variable party (Dutch parties in the 1995 election) into a new variable party6 with six unordered categories: left, social democratic, social liberal, christian democratic, liberal, and strict religious. Categories that do not map onto one of these six groups should become missing. Check the recoding with a cross-tabulation of party against party6.





Fit a multinomial logistic regression of party6 on no predictors (an empty/intercept-only model), using category 1 as the base category. How do you interpret the intercepts?
Refit the same empty model using category 3 as the base category instead. Is there evidence that people are more or less likely to be in category 4 than in category 3?





Create a dummy variable fem for women. Recode religion into a new nominal variable rel4 with four categories. Fit a multinomial logistic regression of party6 on education, rel4, and fem, using category 4 as the base category for party6, and report relative-risk ratios (RRRs). Interpret the RRR for one unit of education for at least one outcome category.
Refit the same model, but this time set category 3 of rel4 as the reference category for that predictor (instead of category 1). Compare the RRRs to the previous model. Why do the RRRs for rel4 change even though the model as a whole fits the data identically?





Fit a multinomial logistic regression of party6 on education, rel4 (with category 1 as reference), and fem, using category 1 as the base category for party6. Compute the average marginal effects of education and fem on the predicted probability of each outcome category.
Refit with category 2 as the reference category for rel4. Compute the average marginal effect of rel4 on the predicted probabilities. Interpret one of these marginal effects.
Compute pairwise comparisons of the marginal effect of rel4 between two specific response categories. Interpret one such pairwise comparison.





Fit the full multinomial model of party6 on education, rel4, and fem. Then refit the model six times, each time excluding all observations belonging to one category of party6. For each of the resulting models, compare the coefficients to those of the full model. For which outcome categories does the exclusion of another category appear to change the coefficients substantially, suggesting that IIA is violated? For which category does IIA appear to hold reasonably well?
Based on your answer to the previous question, what do you conclude overall about whether the IIA assumption holds for this model of party choice?





Recode education into an ordered variable edu4 with four categories. Fit a multinomial model of party6 on edu4 and rel4 (main effects only), using category 1 as the base category.
Refit the model adding the interaction between edu4 and rel4. Test whether this interaction significantly improves the fit, using a likelihood ratio test comparing the two models.
Is there evidence for an interaction between education and religion on party choice? What does — and does not — this tell you about whether education and religion interact in their effect on the predicted probabilities of voting for each party (as opposed to the relative-risk ratios)?
Fit a multinomial model of party6 on education, rel4, and fem (main effects only), and a second model that adds all two-way and three-way interactions between these three predictors. Test whether the full set of interactions significantly improves the fit, using a likelihood ratio test.

Based on your answer to the previous question, what do you conclude overall about whether the IIA assumption holds for this model of party choice?





Recode education into an ordered variable edu4 with four categories. Fit a multinomial model of party6 on edu4 and rel4 (main effects only), using category 1 as the base category.
Refit the model adding the interaction between edu4 and rel4. Test whether this interaction significantly improves the fit, using a likelihood ratio test comparing the two models.
Is there evidence for an interaction between education and religion on party choice? What does — and does not — this tell you about whether education and religion interact in their effect on the predicted probabilities of voting for each party (as opposed to the relative-risk ratios)?
Fit a multinomial model of party6 on education, rel4, and fem (main effects only), and a second model that adds all two-way and three-way interactions between these three predictors. Test whether the full set of interactions significantly improves the fit, using a likelihood ratio test.

13. What the significant interaction does and does not tell you

# There is evidence for an interaction between education and religion on
# the (log) relative-risk ratios describing party choice. This does NOT
# by itself imply that education and religion interact in their effect
# on the predicted *probabilities* of voting for each party -- a
# significant interaction in the relative-risk-ratio formulation does
# not automatically translate into a similarly interpretable interaction
# on the probability scale, because the mapping from relative risks to
# probabilities is nonlinear. If this interaction on the probability
# scale is itself of interest, a more detailed study (e.g. using
# marginal effects and their interactions) would be needed.

title: Multiple linear regression
text:
Use the dataset sesam. We predict postnumb (a post-test score) from age and prenumb (a pre-test score).

Fit a regression of postnumb on age and prenumb. Interpret each coefficient, the intercept, and the adjusted \(R^2\). Is age a significant predictor once prenumb is controlled for?
Compare this result to a simple regression of postnumb on age alone (from the previous chapter). Why can a predictor be significantly related to the outcome in a simple regression, yet not contribute in a multiple regression?
Fit a regression of postnumb on prenumb alone. Compare the coefficient for prenumb and the \(R^2\) to the model that also includes age. What do you conclude?





Use the dataset donations. Treat the “miscellaneous” category of religion as missing, and exclude the corresponding observations from the analyses below (it is too heterogeneous a group to interpret meaningfully).

Test whether average donations differ between religious groups, controlling for income (inc). Fit a regression of donation on religion (as a factor) and inc. Is the overall F-test for the model significant? Which categories differ significantly from the reference category?
Is there a difference in average donation between two specific religious categories that are not both compared to the reference category in the previous output? Use emmeans() for pairwise comparisons between all categories, or refit the model with a different reference category, to answer this.
Yearly donations appear to have been recorded in thousands. Construct a new variable propdon, the proportion of monthly income donated: divide donation (converted to a monthly amount) by monthly income. Report the mean and standard deviation of propdon. What do these values tell you?
Excluding the miscellaneous religion category permanently from the dataset, fit a regression of propdon on religion and obtain post-hoc pairwise comparisons between all categories. Between which categories is there no evidence of a difference?
Use percdon (percentage of income donated) as outcome. Fit a regression on inc alone, and then on inc together with religion. Is there evidence that donations increase with income, even after controlling for religion? Interpret the size of the effect.
Fit a regression of percdon on male, religion, and their interaction. Is there evidence that the effect of religion on donations differs between men and women?
Fit a regression of percdon on inc, religion, and their interaction. Is there evidence that the effect of income on donations varies between religious denominations?
Construct the product of age and lifevent (an indicator for having experienced a serious health problem). Fit a regression of percdon on age, lifevent, and their interaction (both by explicitly creating the product term, and using formula syntax). Is there evidence that the effect of lifevent on donations is larger for older people than for younger people?
Fit a regression of percdon on age, inc, and their interaction. Is there evidence that the effect of income on donations varies with age?
Fit a regression of percdon on male, inc, and their interaction. Is there evidence that the effect of income on donations differs between men and women?
Fit a regression of percdon on male, inc, religion, and all their two-way and three-way interactions. Is there evidence that gender differences in the effect of income on donations vary by religion?




Use the dataset gss91_extended. We study the relationship between years of education (educ) and occupational prestige (prestg80).

Make a scatterplot of prestg80 against educ. Overlay it with both a linear and a quadratic fitted line. Which fits the data better, based on visual inspection?
Fit a regression model of prestg80 on educ, a squared term for educ, and the control variables race, region, and sex. Is the squared term statistically significant? What do you conclude about the shape of the relationship?
Using the coefficients for educ and educ\(^2\), compute the turning point of the curve: the value of educ at which expected prestige is at its minimum or maximum. Is the curve U-shaped or inverted-U shaped? Check how many observations in the data actually fall at or below this turning point, and discuss whether the turning point should be interpreted, or whether it is more appropriate to describe the relationship only over the range where most of the data lie.

text:
Answers

library(haven)
library(emmeans)

Welcome to emmeans.
Caution: You lose important information if you filter this package's results.
See '? untidy'

sesam <- read_dta("data/sesam.dta")
donations <- read_dta("data/donations.dta")
gss91 <- read_dta("data/gss91_extended.dta")


Predicting a post-test score

1. Marginal versus partial effects

fit_multi <- lm(postnumb ~ age + prenumb, data = sesam)
summary(fit_multi)


Call:
lm(formula = postnumb ~ age + prenumb, data = sesam)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-38.130  -6.456  -0.456   5.435  22.568 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   7.4242     5.1854   1.432    0.154    
age           0.1225     0.1084   1.131    0.259    
prenumb       0.7809     0.0637  12.259   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.486 on 237 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4592,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4547 
F-statistic: 100.6 on 2 and 237 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

# Adj. R-squared = 0.45
#
# E(postnumb) = 7.42 + 0.12 age + 0.78 prenumb      (SE_age = 0.11, SE_prenumb = 0.06)
#
# Age does not contribute in predicting postnumb (not significant). The
# marginal correlation between age and postnumb is significant, but here
# the effect of age is conditional on that of prenumb: once you control
# for prenumb, age does not matter.
# If pretest score goes up by 1, posttest score significantly goes up by
# 0.78, irrespective of age.
# People aged 0 with a pretest score of 0 have a posttest score of 7.42;
# interpreting the constant is not meaningful here.
# The F-test p-value is 0.000, so not all coefficients are 0 (R-squared
# is significant). 45% of the variation in the post-test is explained by
# the pre-test and age.


fit_age_only <- lm(postnumb ~ age, data = sesam)
summary(fit_age_only)


Call:
lm(formula = postnumb ~ age, data = sesam)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-33.873  -9.409  -0.818   9.904  27.287 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  -5.8837     6.4681  -0.910    0.364    
age           0.6975     0.1246   5.597 5.98e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.1 on 238 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1163,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1126 
F-statistic: 31.33 on 1 and 238 DF,  p-value: 5.979e-08

# In the simple regression, age is significantly related to postnumb.
# This is because age is correlated with prenumb; once prenumb is added
# to the model, the (partial) effect of age drops out. A predictor can be
# marginally related to Y through its association with other predictors,
# without having an independent (partial) effect once those predictors
# are controlled for.

The correlation between the two predictors is what drives this.

sesam |>
  summarise(r_age_prenumb = cor(age, prenumb, use = "complete.obs"))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  r_age_prenumb
          <dbl>
1         0.433

# older children score higher on the pre-test, which is why age looks
# informative until the pre-test is in the model


fit_prenumb_only <- lm(postnumb ~ prenumb, data = sesam)
summary(fit_prenumb_only)


Call:
lm(formula = postnumb ~ prenumb, data = sesam)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-39.253  -6.283  -0.394   5.796  22.170

(Intercept) 13.08508    1.34795   9.707   <2e-16 ***
prenumb      0.81208    0.05746  14.133   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.492 on 238 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4563,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.454 
F-statistic: 199.7 on 1 and 238 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

# Very little has changed compared to the model with both predictors:
# the coefficient for prenumb and R-squared are almost the same with or
# without age in the model. This confirms that age adds essentially
# nothing once prenumb is controlled for.

A formal test of whether adding age improves the model.

anova(fit_prenumb_only, fit_multi)

    educ 
4.151102

#

# scatterplot (though that plot did not include statistical controls).
# We conclude that around 4 years of education corresponds to the lowest
# predicted prestige.

  summarise(n_at_or_below = sum(educ <= turning_point, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  n_at_or_below
          <int>
1            12

# Only a small number of subjects have educ values at or below the
# turning point (about 12 out of roughly 1500). It is highly unlikely
# that prestige is actually higher with 1 or 2 years of education than
# with 4 years; the model most plausibly applies for 4 and more years of
# education. We therefore abstain from interpreting the turning point
# itself, and conclude instead that, over the range where most of the
# data lie, prestige increases in education at an increasing rate.


gss91 |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    at_or_below = sum(educ <= turning_point, na.rm = TRUE),
    percent = 100 * mean(educ <= turning_point, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
      n at_or_below percent
  <int>       <int>   <dbl>
1  1517          12   0.795

ggplot(gss91, aes(x = educ)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = turning_point, linetype = "dashed")

Warning: Removed 7 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).








# the dashed line marks the turning point
# almost the entire distribution lies to the right of it

The general lesson: a quadratic term is fitted to the whole range of X, but the fit is only trustworthy where the data are dense. A turning point located in a sparse region is an artefact of the functional form you imposed, not a finding about the world.

title: Ordinal logistic regression
text:
Use the dataset hin95_voting.



Construct age (from birthdate), a dummy female, and a recoded church-attendance frequency chfreq (visits per year). Fit an ordered logistic regression of vote (voting intention, an ordinal variable) on education, age, female, and chfreq. Interpret the coefficient for chfreq as an effect on the latent voting-intention variable, and as a change in log odds.
Exponentiate the coefficient for chfreq to obtain an odds ratio. Interpret this odds ratio.
Compute the average marginal effects of all predictors. Interpret the marginal effect of chfreq on each of the four response categories of vote. Why is it not surprising that some of these marginal effects are positive and others negative?





Obtain predicted probabilities for each of the four response categories, for every subject. Verify, for one particular subject, that these probabilities sum to 1 (within rounding error).





Fit a restricted ordinal model without chfreq, and compare it to the full model with chfreq using a likelihood ratio test. What happens if you attempt this directly, without first checking the two models are based on the same sample? Explain why this happens, and how to fix it. After fixing the sample issue, what do you conclude about the relationship between church attendance frequency and voting intention?





Fit three models: (a) chfreq entered linearly, (b) chfreq entered as a fully flexible categorical predictor, and (c) chfreq entered with both a linear and a quadratic term. Compare (a) to (b), and (a) to (c), using likelihood ratio tests. Is there evidence that the linear specification is inadequate?





Fit a model with an interaction between female and chfreq (in addition to the main effects of education, age, female, and chfreq). Is there evidence that the effect of church attendance on voting intention differs between men and women? Report the implied effect of chfreq separately for men and for women.
Confirm your conclusion from the previous question with a likelihood ratio test comparing the model with and without the interaction term.





Compute a pseudo-\(R^2\) for the latent variable underlying vote, using the variance of the fitted linear predictor and the fixed error variance of the ordered logit model (\(\pi^2/3\)).





Test the proportional odds (parallel lines) assumption for the model of vote on education, age, female, and chfreq. Is the assumption supported by the data? What would this mean for the interpretation of the model if the assumption were rejected?

  mutate(

1. The ordered logit model

summary(fit)

# odds of being in a higher (more likely to vote) response category
# rather than a lower one increase by 0.011, holding the other

Type: probs

# If church attendance frequency goes up by 1:
#   - the probability of "certainly voting" increases by about
#     0.2 percentage points
#   - the probability of "probably voting" decreases by about
#     0.1 percentage points
#   - the probability of "probably not voting" decreases by about
#     0.08 percentage points
#   - the probability of "certainly not voting" decreases by about
#     0.06 percentage points
#
# This pattern is not surprising: an increase in the latent
# voting-intention variable shifts probability mass away from the lower
# (less likely to vote) categories toward the higher (more likely to
# vote) category. Because probabilities across all categories must sum
# to 1, some marginal effects are necessarily negative while others are
# positive.




Predicted probabilities

4. Predicted probabilities per response category

pred_probs <- predict(fit, type = "probs")

nrow(hin95_voting)

hin95_voting_pred <- hin95_voting |>
  slice(as.integer(rownames(pred_probs))) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(pred_probs) |> rename_with(~ paste0("pr", seq_along(.))))

# rounding error). Only cases without missing values on any of the
# predictors receive a prediction.




Testing a hypothesis on religion

5. A likelihood ratio test on matching samples

fit_a <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female + chfreq, data = hin95_voting, Hess = TRUE)
fit_b <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female, data = hin95_voting, Hess = TRUE)

# This comparison is not valid:
# tryCatch(lrtest(fit_a, fit_b), error = function(e) e)

# lrtest refuses (or gives a misleading result) if attempted directly,
# because the two models are fit to different samples: fit_a excludes
# cases with a missing value on chfreq, while fit_b does not. A valid
# likelihood ratio test requires both models to be fit to exactly the
# same set of observations.

hin95_voting_complete <- hin95_voting |>
  filter(!is.na(chfreq))

fit_b_matched <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female, data = hin95_voting_complete, Hess = TRUE)
fit_a_matched <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female + chfreq, data = hin95_voting_complete, Hess = TRUE)

lrtest(fit_a_matched, fit_b_matched)

Model 2: vote ~ education + age + female

# religiosity (church attendance frequency), the higher the voting
# intention (LR chi2(1) = 23.27, p < 0.0001).




Checking linearity

6. Linear, flexible, and quadratic specifications

fit_linear <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female + chfreq,
                    data = hin95_voting_complete, Hess = TRUE)

fit_flexible <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female + factor(chfreq),
                      data = hin95_voting_complete, Hess = TRUE)

fit_quadratic <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female + chfreq + I(chfreq^2),
                       data = hin95_voting_complete, Hess = TRUE)

lrtest(fit_linear, fit_flexible)

Explained variance

9. A pseudo-\(R^2\) for the latent variable

fit_r2 <- polr(vote ~ education + age + female + chfreq,
               data = hin95_voting_complete, Hess = TRUE)

# The linear predictor (fitted latent variable, without the error term)
X <- model.matrix(fit_r2)[, -1]
lp <- as.vector(X %*% coef(fit_r2))

var_lp <- var(lp)
r2 <- var_lp / (var_lp + pi^2 / 3)
r2

[1] 0.1037897

# R2 = variance(model) / (variance(model) + variance(error)), where
# variance(error) = pi^2/3 = 3.29 by definition for the ordered logit
# model. This gives a pseudo-R-squared describing the proportion of
# variance explained in the latent (underlying continuous) voting
# intention variable.




Proportional odds assumption

10. The Brant test

brant(fit_r2)

-------------------------------------------- 
Test for    X2  df  probability 
-------------------------------------------- 
Omnibus     36.97   8   0
education   4.93    2   0.09
age     20.45   2   0
female      3.52    2   0.17
chfreq      0.4 2   0.82
-------------------------------------------- 

H0: Parallel Regression Assumption holds

# The Brant test rejects the proportional odds (parallel lines)
# assumption for at least one of the predictors. If this assumption is
# rejected, the effect of that predictor is not the same across all
# cutpoints of vote, and the ordered logit coefficients should be
# interpreted with caution -- a model that relaxes the proportional odds
# assumption (e.g. a generalized/partial proportional odds model) may be
# more appropriate, though such extensions are beyond the scope of this
# course.

title: Model testing
text:
Use the dataset sesam.

Fit a restricted model of postnumb on age and prenumb, and a full model that adds prelet, prerelat, and peabody. Compare the two models with an F-test (anova()). Does adding this set of three predictors significantly improve the fit? How large is the change in \(R^2\)? Is this change of much practical relevance?
Repeat the same test using a Wald test (car::linearHypothesis()) on the full model. Do you reach the same conclusion as with the F-test?
Repeat the same test again using a likelihood ratio test (lmtest::lrtest()) comparing the restricted and full models. Do all three methods agree?
Which of the three added predictors (prelet, prerelat, peabody) is mainly responsible for the improvement in fit? Is this predictor’s effect of much substantive importance, even though it is statistically significant?
Fit the model postnumb ~ prenumb + age separately for boys and for girls (sex == 1 and sex == 2). Compare the coefficient for prenumb between the two groups. Is the effect of prenumb on postnumb, controlling for age, significantly different for boys and girls? (Hint: refit the model as a single regression with an interaction between prenumb and sex, and test the interaction term, rather than comparing the two separate models informally.)




Use the dataset donations. As before, treat the “miscellaneous” category of religion as missing and exclude these observations permanently. Construct propdon, the proportion of monthly income donated, and percdon, this proportion expressed as a percentage. Construct a dummy variable old for subjects older than 40.

Fit a regression of percdon on old and religion (as a factor, with “none” as reference category). Is there evidence that older people (over 40) donate a larger share of their income than younger people, controlling for religion?
Fit a regression of percdon on male and religion. Is there evidence that men donate a larger share of their income than women, controlling for religion? Comment on the strength of the evidence if the p-value is close to, but not below, 0.05.
Using the model from the previous question, test whether religion as a whole contributes to explaining percdon, controlling for gender. Do this in at least two ways: (a) a joint test of all religion coefficients in the full model (e.g. car::linearHypothesis() or anova() on a single model with drop1()), and (b) comparing a restricted model without religion to the full model with religion, using anova(). Do the two approaches agree?
Fit a regression of percdon on social integration (socint) alone. Is there evidence that donations increase with social integration? Now add religion to the model. What happens to the coefficient for socint? What does this tell you about the relationship between social integration, religion, and donations?
Fit a restricted model of percdon on lifevent alone, and a full model that adds religion. Compare the two models with an F-test. Is there evidence that people who experienced a serious health problem (lifevent = 1) donate a larger share of their income than those who did not, controlling for religion?
Fit a regression of percdon on inc alone, and then on inc together with religion. Is there evidence that donations increase with income, even after controlling for religion? Interpret the size of the effect.
Construct the interaction between male and socint. Fit a regression of percdon on male, socint, and their interaction. Is the effect of social integration on donations different for men and women? Use margins-style predictions (e.g., compute the predicted slope of socint separately for each value of male from the fitted coefficients) to describe the effect separately for men and women.
Fit a regression of percdon on male, years of education (edu), and their interaction. Is there evidence that the effect of education on donations differs between men and women?
Fit a regression of percdon on male, lifevent, and their interaction. Is there evidence that the effect of having experienced a serious health problem on donations differs between men and women?

title: Random sampling data
text:
Load the dataset world95.
Take a random sample of 25% of the observations:

world95_sample <- world95 |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.25)

Obtain the mean and variance of a variable that interests you (by now you know or can find out what function to use to obtain summary statistics). Copy these numbers to paper.
Reload the dataset world95; take again a sample of 25%; and obtain again the average and variance of the same variable. Convince yourself that you understand why these numbers are different.
Note that the sample sizes of the random samples are the same. The samples were drawn WITHOUT replacement. You may also express that you want 30 observations selected at random (and without replacement) from the 109 observations contained in the full dataset.

world95_sample <- world95 |>
  slice_sample(n = 30)

A different sampling strategy is to select each observation independently with probability 0.25 (see rbinom()). Now the actual sample size that is obtained will be random, on average 0.25 × 109, but with some chance variation. Convince yourself that the actual sample size is not constant across replications.

world95_sample <- world95 |>
  filter(rbinom(n(), 1, 0.25) == 1)

If you redo an analysis multiple times on a random sample, you will obtain different results each time. This is often not what you want. Thus, often it is better to ensure that the same random numbers are generated.

set.seed(13579)

Sampling from data has many applications. When you analyze a very big dataset, software may take quite a long time reading data and computing the quantities of interest. To get a good feeling for the data one may look at a random selection of the data. Final analyses may subsequently be performed using the full dataset.
A more advanced use of (re)sampling from a dataset is the bootstrap, a modern method for making inferences from data relying less on strong assumptions and mathematics and more on intensive computer calculations.

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
In this section, we use ggplot2 to create basic graphs in R. The examples use the built-in mpg dataset from the ggplot2 package.
library(tidyverse)

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Scatterplots
Scatterplots are useful for studying relationships between numerical variables.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()








A regression line can be added with geom_smooth().

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Histograms
Histograms show the distribution of one numerical variable.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram()








You can change the bin width.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Density plots
Density plots show a smoother version of a distribution.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_density()

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Bar charts
Bar charts are useful for categorical variables.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar()

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Grouping with color
You can use color to show groups within the same graph.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point()

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Faceting
Faceting creates separate panels for different groups.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ class)

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Labels
Good graphs need clear labels.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Fuel efficiency by engine size",
    x = "Engine displacement",
    y = "Highway miles per gallon"
  )

title: Data visualization with ggplot2
text:
Themes
Themes change the appearance of the graph.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()








The goal of a graph is to make the data easier to understand. Always choose a graph that fits the type of variable and the question you want to answer.

title: Selecting cases
text: In this part you will learn about selecting cases (observations).

title: Selecting cases
text:
R
Examples:
Select observations using logical conditions:

data |>   
  filter(sex == 1)
# select observations for which sex equals 1

data |>   
  filter(sex == 1, edu > 3)
# select observations for which sex equals 1 AND edu is larger than 3

data |>   
  filter(sex == 1 | edu >= 3)
# select observations for which sex equals 1 OR edu is at least 3
# the vertical bar means OR, so respondents satisfying either condition are counted


data |> 
  filter(edu != 3)
# select observations in which edu is different than 3


data |> 
  filter((sex == 1 & edu > 3) | (sex == 0 & edu < 3))
# select observations in which one of this is true:
# 1. sex equals 1 and edu is larger than 3
# OR
# 2. sex equals 0 and education is lower than 3

data |> 
  filter(age == max(age))
# select observation(s) whose age equals the maximum age in the dataset, i.e. the 
# oldest person(s). Should use na.rm=TRUE is there are missing values in age

Select observations based on row number:

data |> 
   slice(5) 
# select 5th row

data |>   
  slice(1:20) 
# select rows 1 to 20

data |>   
  slice_head(20)
# select first 20 observations (same as above)

data |>   
  slice_tail(20)
# select the last 20 observations  

The same can also be done with filter() and row_number():

data |>   
  filter(row_number() == 5) 
# select 5th row 

data |>   
  filter(row_number() <= 20)  
# select the first 20 observations

data |>   
  filter(row_number() > (n() - 20))
# select the last 20 observations 
# n() gives the total number of rows

Keep a subset of observations:

data_male <- data |>   
  filter(male == 1)  
# create a new dataset containing only observations for which male==1

data_first100 <- data |>   
  slice(1:100)
# create a new dataset containing only the first 100 observations

The argument .by is to apply a filter within groups. This is useful when you want to compare an observation with other observations in each group, and filter based on that. You will learn more about grouped operations in Aggregating data. Suppose each observation belongs to a household, indicated by the id variable hh_id:

data |>   
  filter(row_number() == 1, .by = hh_id)  
# select the first row from *each household*. It is as if we create one dataset per 
# household, selected the first row from each of them, them put them together again

data |>   
  filter(age == max(age), .by = hh_id)  
# select observations where age equals the maximum age *within each household*, i.e. 
# the oldest in each household. Note that this can be more than one person per household
# if they have the same age.

title: Creating a system file from raw data
text:
In this part you learn about reading raw data into R. Raw data are often stored as text files that can be opened using a simple text editor. Typically the data are in the form of a data matrix in which the rows are cases, columns are variables, and values are separated by commas, tabs, or spaces.
In modern R workflows, raw data are usually read from files such as CSV, tab-delimited text files, Excel files, or Stata files. Occasionally, it is also useful to create a small dataset manually in R, for example for examples, tests, or teaching.

title: Creating a system file from raw data
text:
R
In this part you need to learn and read about the following R functions:



Function
Description




read_csv()
Read comma-separated text data


read_tsv()
Read tab-separated text data


read_table()
Read whitespace-separated text data


read_dta()
Read a Stata dataset


write_csv()
Save data as a CSV file


write_rds()
Save data as an R object


tribble()
Manually create a small dataset


View()
Inspect a dataset in RStudio



Examples:
Read a CSV file:

library(readr)
data <- read_csv("data/mydata.csv")

Read a tab-delimited text file:

data <- read_tsv("data/mydata.txt")

Read a whitespace-separated text file:

data <- read_table("data/mydata.dat")

Read a Stata dataset:

library(haven)
data <- read_dta("data/mydata.dta")

Create a small dataset manually:

library(tibble)
data <- tribble(
  ~hrespnr, ~city,        ~female, ~edu,
  101,      "Amsterdam",  1,       3,
  103,      "Den Haag",   0,       5,
  107,      "Rotterdam",  0,       2,
  109,      "Utrecht",    1,       3
)

Inspect the dataset:

View(data)

Save the dataset as a CSV file:

write_csv(data, "data/mydata.csv")

Save the dataset as an R object:

write_rds(data, "data/mydata.rds")

1. Manual entering data
Enter the data by hand with tribble().

mydata <- tribble(
  ~hrespnr, ~city,        ~female, ~edu,
  101,      "Amsterdam",  1,       3,
  103,      "Den Haag",   0,       5,
  107,      "Rotterdam",  0,       2,
  109,      "Utrecht",    1,       3
)

4     109 Utrecht        1     3

# tribble() lays the data out row by row, so the code looks like the table
# the column names are preceded by a tilde

Check what R made of the variable types.

glimpse(mydata)

# city is a character variable; the other three are numeric (dbl)
# note that hrespnr and female are identifiers and codes, not quantities,
# even though R stores them as numbers

Save this version.

write_rds(mydata, "data/mydata_tribble.rds")
# .rds keeps the object exactly as it is, including variable types

Now build the same dataset as a CSV file. Writing the file from R is the reproducible way to do it; you could equally well type it in a text editor and save it as data/mydata.csv.

csv_text <- "hrespnr,city,female,edu
101,Amsterdam,1,3
103,Den Haag,0,5
107,Rotterdam,0,2
109,Utrecht,1,3
"

write_file(csv_text, "data/mydata.csv")
# the first line holds the variable names, each following line is one case
# values are separated by commas, without spaces after them

  cat()

A remark on types. read_csv() guesses the type of each column from its contents, whereas tribble() takes the types from what you typed. Here both give the same result, but a guess can go wrong: an identifier with leading zeros, such as a postcode 0234, would be read as the number 234. You can override the guess.

mydata_typed <- read_csv(
  "data/mydata.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    hrespnr = col_character(),
    city = col_character(),
    female = col_double(),
    edu = col_double()
  )
)

# hrespnr is now text, which is what an identifier really is

Finally, a note on why .rds and .csv are both useful. A CSV file can be opened by any program and read by anyone, but it stores only text and loses the variable types. An .rds file preserves the R object exactly, but only R can read it.

list.files("data", pattern = "^mydata")

title: Factor analysis (FA)
text:
R
You need to learn about the following R functions for factor analysis. They are part of the psych package, which needs to be installed and loaded. Optionally you may want to check principal component analysis.



R
Description




fa()
factor analysis by maximum likelihood


scree()
plot of eigenvalues to determine number of factors



Examples:
Setup data on sex role attitudes

library(psych)
library(haven)

data <- read_dta("data/sbs399_sexroles.dta")
# this dataset contains 5 items about sex role attitudes, in a 5-point Likert format
# Important: in the code below we use the entire data object because it already contains only the 5 items. 
# If you have a larger dataset, you need to select the relevant items first.

Examine correlation between items:

cor(
  data,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
)

Determine the number of factors graphically with a scree plot:

scree(data)

Factor analysis using maximum likelihood:

fa_fit <- fa(
  data,
  nfactors = 2,
  fm = "ml"
)

Rotate common factors to ease interpretation.

fa_varimax <- fa(
  data,
  nfactors = 2,
  fm = "ml",
  rotate = "varimax"
)

fa_oblique <- fa(
  data,
  nfactors = 2,
  fm = "ml",
  rotate = "promax"
)

Print the factor loadings (pattern matrix):

fa_varimax$loadings

Print the structure matrix:

fa_varimax$Structure

Get factor scores:

fa_scores <- fa_varimax$scores

title: Factor analysis (FA)
text:
Assignments

Muslim rights
Use the dataset muslimrights. The dataset contains two sets of items.
Attitudes towards Muslim expressive rights was measured with seven statements. Four example items were:

The right to establish Islamic schools should always exist in the Netherlands.
Some Islamic holidays should become official Dutch holidays.
Dutch TV should broadcast more programmes by and for Muslims.
In the Netherlands the wearing of a headscarf should not be forbidden.

National identification was measured by six statements:

My Dutch identity is an important part of my self (iden1);
I identify strongly with the Netherlands (iden2);
I feel a strong attachment to the Netherlands (iden3);
I am proud of my Dutch background (iden4);
Being Dutch is a very important part of how I see myself (iden5); and
I feel a strong sense of belonging to the Netherlands (iden6).

We will focus on the first set of items, right1 to right7.

Check the descriptives. Check the frequencies. Are the variables approximately normally distributed? Why is this important?
Do an EFA/ML of the data, first with an unrotated solution (rotate = "none"). Then apply a varimax rotation.
Provide interpretations:


For the moment we choose two dimensions, even though the scree plot might suggest a different number. In the unrotated solution, how much variance is explained by factor 1 and factor 2? And in the rotated solution? Verify that the sum of the variances of factors 1 and 2 is the same for the unrotated and rotated solutions.
Which variable is not very well explained by the two factors?
Interpret the two factors, using the varimax rotation.

Tip: plotting the factor loadings may help you interpret the factors. Assuming the object created with fa() is called fa_varimax, you can plot the loadings with plot(fa_varimax, labels = rownames(fa_varimax$loadings)).

If you would make two sum scores for the items, which variables go into sum score 1 and which in sum score 2?
Apply a promax rotation. Provide interpretations:

What is the correlation between the factors?
Interpret the two factors.
Which variables go into each of the factors?



Oversee all analyses that you carried out. What is your final conclusion with respect to the number of dimensions (factors)? Assume for the moment that you choose two dimensions, what is your final conclusion with respect to the interpretation of the dimensions?
Optional. Analyze the 6 items about national identification in the dataset.



Bem Sex Role Inventory
BSRI stands for the Bem Sex Role Inventory (Bem, 1974). We have data from a sample of 369 middle-class, English speaking women between the ages of 21 and 60 who were interviewed face-to-face. The data are provided by Tabacknick and Fidell (2007), Using multivariate statistics, 5nd ed., Boston: Pearson. The full inventory takes 60 items. Tabachnick and Fidell state that in our data there are 20 items measuring the overall trait femininity, 20 items the overall trait masculinity, and 5 items measuring the overall trait social desirability. The question format is that respondents are asked to attribute the 60 traits to themselves using scores going from 1 (“never or almost never true of me”) to 7 (“always or almost always true of me”). It turns out that the data are not thoroughly cleaned, as occasionally there appears a 0 and a 9 in the data file. We ignore this problem.

Do an initial check on the data using frequencies and descriptives. Notice that some of the variables are skewed. Skewness of items lowers the maximum that correlations can attain.
Produce a scree plot. It is clear that that the elbow criterion is not easy to use here. Clearly there are two outstanding factors. If we take factor 3, then we should also take 4 and 5 as their eigenvalues are close to the eigenvalue of 3. We may even consider factors 6 and 7. We will have a look at two different solutions: two factors and five factors.
Do an EFA/ML with two factors with a promax rotation. Notice that the correlation between the rotated factors is relatively low. Interpret the two factors.
Do another EFA/ML, now with five factors and a promax rotation. Interpret the five factors using only those variables that have loadings larger than .40. You can do this by using print(your_fa_object$loadings, cutoff = .40).

We stop here. We have seen that interpreting the factor structure for such a large list of items is difficult and sometimes somewhat arbitrary. More insight could be found from validating the factors in experimental research and by correlating the factors to other variables. Of course, this is beyond the scope of this course.

title: Documenting data
text: In this short section you will learn about the following basic tasks:

title: Documenting data
text:
R
Learn the following R commands to document the data, variables, and values:



Function
Description




rename()
Rename variables


mutate()
Modify or create variables


factor()
Convert a variable to a factor


na_if()
Change a specific value to NA


replace_na()
Replace NA with a specific value


relocate()
Change the order of variables



Rename variables:

data <- data |> 
  rename(educ = v101) 
# rename v101 to educ

data <- data |> 
  rename(sex = v1, edu = v2) 
# rename multiple variables

Convert a categorical variable to a factor:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("male", "female")
    )
  )
# assign meaningful labels to categories

Code missing values:

data <- data |> 
  mutate(educ = na_if(educ, 99)) 
# change the value 99 to NA 

data <- data |> mutate(across(c(educ, feduc), ~ na_if(.x, 9))) 
# change the value 9 to NA in educ and feduc

Replace missing values with a numeric code:

data <- data |> 
  mutate(educ = replace_na(educ, 99)) 
# change NA to 99

Change the order of variables:

data <- data |> 
  relocate(hrespnr, sex, age, edu) 
# put these variables first 

Be careful when replacing missing values with numeric codes such as 99. In R, missing values should usually be coded as NA. Numeric missing-value codes can easily be treated as real values in analyses if they are not recoded properly.

title: Documenting data
text:
Assignments
In these assignments we use the dataset sbs399_unlabeled.dta.

Rename the variable hrespnr to hid and the variable hrinc to hinc in one command.
The variable sex is coded numerically. Convert sex into a factor with meaningful labels. Use male and female as category labels.
The variables sexrol1 and sexrol2 measure family attitudes. Convert both variables into factors with the following category labels:

fully disagree
slightly disagree
indifferent
slightly agree
fully agree

title: Documenting data
text:
Answers

1. Rename the variable hrespnr to hid and the variable hrinc to hinc in one command.

data <- data |>
  rename(
    hid = hrespnr,
    hinc = hrinc
  )



2. The variable sex is coded numerically. Convert sex into a factor with meaningful labels. Use male and female as category labels.

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("male", "female")
    )
  )



3. The variables sexrol1 and sexrol2 measure family attitudes. Convert both variables into factors with the following category labels: fully disagree, slightly disagree, indifferent, slightly agree, fully agree.

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    sexrol1 = factor(
      sexrol1,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "fully disagree",
        "slightly disagree",
        "indifferent",
        "slightly agree",
        "fully agree"
      )
    ),
    sexrol2 = factor(
      sexrol2,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "fully disagree",
        "slightly disagree",
        "indifferent",
        "slightly agree",
        "fully agree"
      )
    )
  )

title: Adding cases and variables
text:
In this chapter, you will learn about how to combine different datasets:
We will elaborate on and illustrate these tasks with simple examples. As a first example, you organize an international data collection, where all countries use the same questionnaire. You obtain datasets from the Netherlands, from the UK, etc. The datasets contain (largely) the same variables. You want to make one dataset of these country datasets, with an additional variable country recording the data source.
As a second example, we consider that the two files to be combined contain different variables. We need to distinguish two cases:
A crucial concept in merging is a key. A key comprises one or more variables used to match observations from the two datasets. In the example of one-to-one merging, the key is likely a country identifier. In the example on many-to-one merging, the key is the city identifier. The key variable or variables should occur in both datasets. In R, key variables do not necessarily need to have the same name in both datasets, but using the same name is usually clearer and less error-prone.
PS: The first type of merge is also possible without a key variable or key variables, and strictly on sequential order of the files: the first record of file A with the first record of file B, the second record of file A with the second record of file B, etc. This type of merging is very error prone. We urge you never to merge without keys.

title: Adding cases and variables
text:
R
You should read about the following R functions:



Function
Description




bind_rows()
Append datasets, add cases


left_join()
Merge datasets, add variables



We present an R snippet for the four tasks:

Add cases

oecd <- bind_rows(
  world95_oecd_eu,
  world95_oecd_extra
)



one-to-one merge

countries <- left_join(
              world95_3_pop,
              world95_3_rel,
              by = "country" 
            )

Note that in left_join(), the argument by specifies the key variable. If the key variable has the same name in both datasets, you can omit the argument by, but it is good practice to include it for clarity. If the key variable has different names in the two datasets, you can specify them as a named vector, e.g., by = c("country" = "country_name"). If the key is a composite, you can specify multiple variables, e.g., by = c("country", "year").


one-to-many merge

individuals <-  left_join(
                  merge_indiv,
                  world95_3_pop,
                  by = "country"
                )



All combinations of parents and schools
Note that “many-to-many” merges are relatively rare, and creating all combinations of units (which multiplies the number of rows) is very often not what you want. This is why in the code below we have to explicitly tell left_join() that we know what we are doing and really want a many-to-many merge; otherwise it will still produce the combinations but throw a warning.

# Let's specify a fake join key, with the same for all values in both datasets
schools <- schools |>
            mutate(join_key = 1)

parents <- parents |>
            mutate(join_key = 1)

pairs <- left_join(
              parents,
              schools,
              by = "join_key",
              relationship = "many-to-many",
            ) |>
          select(-join_key)


# A more compact way, using tidyr::crossing():
# (will fail if there are variables with the same name in both datasets, line "join_key",
# but can be fixed with the .name_repair argument)
crossing(parents, join_key)

Some notes on combining datasets

To append datasets, make sure that corresponding variables in both datasets have the same names, and are coded in the same way. For example, you do not want sex to be coded 0 = male and 1 = female in one dataset, and 0 = female and 1 = male in the other.
Issues to consider with key variables for merging:

Make sure that the keys are coded identically in both datasets. If you merge on country, a given country code should obviously refer to the same country in both datasets.
In a 1:1 merge, make sure to always use a key, e.g., the respondent number. Do not rely on the assumption that the first observation in one dataset corresponds with the first observation in the other dataset.
R allows composite keys for merging, i.e., the key may consist of multiple variables, e.g., country and year.
Do not merge on keys with missing values, unless you really know what you are doing.
left_join() keeps all observations from the first dataset and adds matching information from the second dataset. Observations in the first dataset without a match receive NA on the variables from the second dataset.
As always: Do not assume that combining files was successful if R does not complain. Check the number of observations! Check the variables! Check values! Check everything!

title: Adding cases and variables
text:
Assignments

1. Synthetic Eurobarometer data
The datasets eurobaro2000_ge, eurobaro2000_nl, and eurobaro2000_uk contain subsets of the Eurobarometer 2000 data, with small selections of respondents from Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. These datasets comprise demographic information of respondents, sex and age, and their trust in two institutions of the European Union, the EU commission, tcomm, and the EU parliament, tparl, recorded using 5 point scales. Use bind_rows() to append these three datasets to create one dataset eb2000 for the three countries, adding a string variable country recording the data source. Add a year variable that includes the value 2000.
The datasets eurobaro2002 and eurobaro2004 similarly contain Eurobarometer data for the same three countries for the years 2002 and 2004. We want you to combine these two datasets with eb2000. Make sure that the in the combined dataset there is a variable contaning the year of each survey. However, there are some complications that you have to deal with.

the variable Country in 2002: The United Kingdom is not abbreviated to UK as in 2000. (Also note the variable name)
the variable country in 2004: It is a labelled numeric variable, not a string variable.
the variable sex in 2002 and 2004: The meaning of 1 and 2 are reversed compared to 2000. Use the coding of 2000.
in 2002 and 2004, trust was also measured for the European Court of Law.
in 2004, trust was measured on a binary scale, 0 = no and 1 = yes, rather than on the 5 point scale used in 2000 and 2002. We do not want to discard information, but also should not bind columns whose values represent different things. Think of a solution and implement it.

We also have two contextual datasets. eudata contains the population size (in September 2012, ignore the mismatch) of these EU countries. The dataset euydata describes the GDP in some EU countries in the years 2000 to 2004, rounded in 1000 EUR units. Make sure you check thge variable names and values before joining. Enrich the individual data with these two contextual datasets using left_join().


2. Add cases: appending datasets
In this assignment we consider how to combine observations from multiple files. For instance, data entry from paper questionnaires is performed by different people, yielding different datasets with the same variables for different subjects.

As this exercise is meant to develop your computer skills, we are going to generate two disjoint sets of records ourselves. Load sbs399. Select the men and save them in the object sbs399m. Then select the women and save them in the object sbs399f.
To reconstruct the full dataset sbs399 from these two partial datasets on women and men respectively, append the files using bind_rows(). Check that the number of cases is unchanged.
Now do a more complicated append of the files involving different subjects and partially different variables. To simulate this, delete some variables from the male file and some other variables from the female file. Append the files using bind_rows(). How does R deal with the variables that appear in one dataset, but not in the other?



3. 1:1 merge: adding variables
In this assignment, we consider how to combine multiple files that comprise different variables for the same subjects. In real life, this may for instance occur in a panel study, in which data from different waves are stored in separate files. We require you create such datasets for training purposes.

Use isbs399. This is a variant of sbs399 in which we excluded same-sex households. If you want to, you may consider constructing isbs399 from sbs399 yourself. This dataset comprises couples nested in households and singles. Respondents are identified with hrespnr. Save two subsets of isbs399, one with the variables irespnr, hrespnr, sex, ybirth, and age; the other with irespnr, hrespnr, sex, fage, and fpres.
Merge the two files you just created, using irespnr as the key and left_join(). Ascertain that the merged file is correct.
Now create the two subsets of isbs399 again, excluding the first observation in the first file, and the second observation in the second file. Merge again on hrespnr using left_join(). Inspect the first two observations. What do you conclude?

Extra: experiment with full_join() instead of left_join(). What do you conclude?

Merge the two datasets once more, this time matching on hrespnr. Why does it not work? Yes, hrespnr does not uniquely identify observations. The pair hrespnr and sex does uniquely identify subjects, and so they make a valid composite key. Merge on the pair hrespnr and sex, and convince yourself that this leads to the same result as merging on hrespnr.



4. n:1 merge: contextual enrichment
In this assignment we consider how to enrich an individual level dataset with contextual data. The dataset sbs399 contains information on individuals nested in couples or households, identified by the household identifier hrespnr. The dataset hin95_house provides properties of the couple’s house, ownership, number of rooms, etc. Thus, hin95_house also contains the household identifier.
Merge sbs399 and hin95_house on hrespnr using left_join().


5. Cities and regions
We consider a partially synthetic example with three datasets. The dataset mm_hn95data contains information about households, including the city of residence, and the cities in which the husband and wife work. The second dataset mm_cities contains information about cities, including the region to which the city belongs. The third dataset mm_regions contains information about regions. For your convenience, we list the variables in the three datasets.

mm_hn95data

hhid household id
city city of residence
hhinc household income
nkids number of kids
hrace husband: race
hwcity work husband: city
wrace wife: race
wwcity work wife: city
religion religion of couple
vchurch frequency church visit couple

mm_cities

cityid city identifier
inhabit number of inhabitants
region region identifier
jobs number of jobs
vacant number of vacancies

mm_regions

regid region identifier
growth economic growth in 1990

Start with the dataset on households mm_hn95data. Merge in properties of the city in which the households live from the dataset mm_cities using left_join().
Continuing with this merged dataset, now add the economic growth in the region of residence from the dataset mm_regions using left_join().
We start again with the unmodified dataset mm_hn95data. This dataset contains the ids of three cities relevant to the households: the city in which they live, city, the city in which the husband works, hwcity, and the city in which the wife works, wwcity. We want you to merge in information about each of the cities, adding three variables, e.g., named res_inhabit, hwcity_inhabit, and wwcity_inhabit, for the number of inhabitants in each of the cities. Use left_join() multiple times.

title: Getting to know and summarizing data
text:
In this part you will learn about the following basic tasks:
The concept of key variables may be new to you. A key consists of one or more variables that uniquely identify observations.
In social science datasets, we often use single observations to represent all variables measured on subjects. Each person is then a row in the data matrix. Such datasets often contain a respondent number, say id, usually integer valued. The values of id are usually unique, and then id qualifies as a key. If you know a subject’s value of id, you can find the corresponding row in the data matrix, and hence know all the subject’s characteristics.
If a value of id occurs more than once, obviously, the value of id does not identify a unique subject, and id is not a key. Observe that id need not take all possible values. For instance, if your id consists of 9 digits, likely your dataset does not contain all possible numbers of 9 digits. Many possible values of id will not be used. That is not a problem. id would still be a key if all values are distinct.
If id takes duplicate values, we may form a key by considering additional variables. For instance, think of a household survey with one or two adults. Observations are people nested in households. The variable hid, household number, would not be a key. The combination of hid and sex might be a key if the sample comprises single people and different-sex couples, but not if the sample also includes same-sex couples, cohabiting siblings, etc. In the latter case, the data may contain a variable indicating whether a person is the oldest adult in the household, and together with hid this variable may form a key. If you only have birth dates, the combination of hid and birth date is usually a key, but you could have bad luck if your data include a household with two cohabiting twin sisters.
If a dataset does not contain a case identifier such as a respondent number, we strongly suggest you create one. Be sure to do this in a reproducible way. First put the observations in a specific order, by sorting on a series of variables that uniquely identify cases. In the example below, we assume that each observation has a unique pattern on the variables city, age, edu, and sex. Obviously, you should verify this assumption.
In R, you can check duplicates and create an identifier as follows:
After sorting the cases, a new variable is created with the value 1 in the first observation, 2 in the second observation, 3 in the third observation, etc. This is one of the occasions in which you may want to save the dataset, but we urge you not to overwrite the original file.

title: Getting to know and summarizing data
text:
R
You will learn the R functions listed below to describe and summarize data. Read the corresponding documentation pages when needed. Start with the description and examples. We do not expect you to learn all functions by heart, but you should get a rough idea of, and remember, what they can accomplish.







Function
Description




read_csv()
Load a CSV file into R


read_dta() / read_sav()
Load a Stata / SPSS file into R


read_excel()
Load an Excel file into R


glimpse()
Describe data contents


skim()
Describe data contents and summary statistics


View()
View observations and variables


arrange()
Sort observations


table()
One-way and two-way tables of frequencies


prop.table()
Convert frequencies to proportions


tabyl()
Frequency tables with percentages


chisq.test()
Pearson’s chi-square test for independence


summarise()
Summary statistics


cor()
Correlations (Pearson by default)


count()
Count observations by category or group


select()
Select variables


filter()
Select observations satisfying a condition


slice()
Select observations by row number



Examples:
Load a file into memory, using a relative path:

library(readr) # for opening CSV files 
data <- read_csv("data/mydata.csv")  

library(haven) # for opening Stata (.dta) and SPSS (.sav) files 
data <- read_dta("data/mydata.dta")  
data <- read_sav("data/mydata.sav") 

library(readxl) # for opening Excel (.xlsx) files 
data <- read_excel("data/mydata.xlsx") 

Describe variables in the active dataset:

glimpse(data) # shows basic info about the dataset and 
              # a overview of all variables

data |>   
  select(edu, exp) |>   
  glimpse() # compact overview of edu and exp  

data |>   
  select(starts_with("rat")) |>   
  glimpse() # describe all variables starting with rat 

skim(data) # summary statistics  (from package 'skimr')
View(data) # open data viewer in RStudio 

List observations:

data # all variables and all observations  

data |>   
  select(edu, inc) # selection of variables  

data |>   
  filter(country == 4) # selection of observations 
                       # (all rows in which variable 'country' equals 4)

data |>   
  select(country, edu, inc) |>    # selection of variables
  slice(1:20)                     # selection of observations 1 to 20 

Sort observations on one or more variables:

data |>   
  arrange(edu) # sort by edu (increasing)

data |>   
  arrange(edu, inc) # sort by edu and inc  (increasing)

data |>   
  arrange(desc(edu)) # sort by edu (decreasing)

One-way tabulation, frequencies:

table(data$class) # one-way table  

table(data$edu, useNA = "ifany") # one-way table, include missing values  

# usign tabyl, from package 'janitor'
data |> 
  tabyl(edu) # frequency table with missing values and percentages

Two-way tabulation of variables:

table(data$edu, data$class)

# using tabyl:
data |> 
  tabyl(edu, class)

Row and column percentages:

# row percentages:
table(data$edu, data$class) |> 
  prop.table(margin = 1)
# column percentages:
table(data$edu, data$class) |> 
  prop.table(margin = 2)

# using tabyl:
data |> 
  tabyl(edu, class) |> 
  adorn_percentages("row")

data |> 
  tabyl(edu, class) |> 
  adorn_percentages("columns") |> 
  adorn_pct_formatting() # optional

In prop.table, the argument margin = 1 computes proportions within rows, while margin = 2 computes proportions within columns.
Pearson’s chi-square test for independence:

table(data$edu, data$class) |> 
  chisq.test()
# Pearson's chi-square test for independence

The chi-square test checks whether two categorical variables are statistically independent.
Tabulation of three or more variables:

# three variables 
xtabs(~ edu + class + gender, data = data, addNA=TRUE) 

data |> 
  tabyl(edu, class, gender)

# four variables (not possible with tabyl)
xtabs(~ edu + class + gender + country, data = data, addNA=TRUE) 

# It is also possible to obtain frequencies using count(). 
# But it is not printed as a table and it does not show missing combinations 
data |>   
  count(gender, edu, class)

data |>   
  count(country, gender, edu, class)  

Summary statistics:

# Summary statistics for income 
data |> 
  skim(income)

data |>   
  summarise(     
    mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE),     
    sd_income = sd(income, na.rm = TRUE),     
    min_income = min(income, na.rm = TRUE),     
    max_income = max(income, na.rm = TRUE)   
    ) 

Correlation matrix of two or more variables:

data |>   
  select(edu, inc, age) |>   
  cor(use = "complete.obs") # Pearson correlations 

Count the number of observations meeting a condition (you will practice this again in Selecting cases):

# count observations with income above 50000:
data |>   
  filter(income > 50000) |>   
  nrow() 

# count observations with income between 5000 and 50000, boundaries excluded: 
data |>   
  filter(income > 5000, income < 50000) |>   
  nrow()

# count observations with income between 5000 and 50000, boundaries included:
data |>   
  filter(income >= 5000, income <= 50000) |> # alternative: filter(between(income, 5000, 50000))  
  nrow() 

# count observations with income above 50000 and income not missing:
data |>   
  filter(income > 50000, !is.na(income)) |>   
  nrow() 

Check that the variable birthd is a key:

data |>   
  summarise(no_missing = all(!is.na(birthd))) # birthd is never missing  

data |>   
  count(birthd) |>   
  filter(n > 1) # check duplicates in birthd 

Check that birthd and sex form a composite key:

data |>   
  summarise(no_missing = all(!is.na(birthd), !is.na(sex))) # birthd and sex are never missing  

data |>   
  count(birthd, sex) |>   
  filter(n > 1) # check duplicates in the combination of birthd and sex 

Create a key:

data <- data |>   
  arrange(birthd, sex) |>   
  mutate(id = row_number()) # create id after sorting by birthd and sex
